<!-- /world/terrain-generation/ -->

<a id="world-terrain-generation"></a>

## Terrain generation

> **In short:**
> where a chunk comes from, and everything a script can do about
> it. `world.on_generate` fills each chunk of a script world, `world.on_populate`
> adds to the engine's overworld, `noise` and biomes shape it, `terrain` in
> citadel.yml rewrites the a0.1.0 populate list, and `world.generate` declares a
> whole world as rules the engine builds on every core with no script per chunk.


## Where a chunk comes from

The `world` key in the pack's manifest says where a chunk comes from:

| `world` key | Chunks |
| --- | --- |
| `"script"` | `world.on_generate` makes them. A chunk it does not fill is air. |
| `"overworld"` | Citadel's terrain: biomes, hills, caves, ores, trees, sea level 63. Scripts only add to it (`world.on_populate`). `seed` pins the map. |
| any other name | A world folder in the pack — `<pack>/hub` for `world: hub` — made once from a build or a vanilla world. The server reads it chunk by chunk and saves player changes into it. A chunk the folder lacks comes from `world.on_generate`, or is air. |
| no key | The scripts are asked first. A chunk no script filled is overworld terrain on a `mode: full` server and air on a `mode: lite` server. |

**Chunks nobody is near are unloaded.** Every ten seconds the server drops
chunks beyond the view distance of all players and entities. When someone
returns, a stored world loads the chunk from disk (a changed chunk waits for
its save); a `script` world calls `on_generate` again. The chunks around the
spawn are generated before the port opens.

The world's `level.json` keeps the seed, spawn, time and weather of the first
run. Changing `seed` does nothing to an existing world — delete the world
folder for a new map. A reload keeps the world: a changed `world.on_generate`,
`seed` or `terrain` applies only to chunks generated from here on.

## `on_generate`

[`world.on_generate(fn: (chunk: Chunk) -> ())`](#ref-World-on_generate) is
called for a chunk each time it comes into memory, in a script world. It is a
**single-handler setter**: a later call replaces the previous handler, and it
returns nothing.

> **Gotcha:**
> because chunks unload and generate again, `on_generate` must make
> the same blocks every time. Draw from a hash of the position, never
> `math.random`. A script-world chunk changed live (`world.set_block`,
> `world.fill`) stays in memory.


Chunk callbacks keep their own **2 s limit**, separate from the tick budget —
and the engine waits **60 s** for a chunk; a chunk that is not ready then is
air. That wait is what lets a generator fetch data over `http` inside
`on_generate`; make the chunk without the data when the fetch fails.

## `on_populate`

[`world.on_populate(fn: (chunk: Chunk) -> ())`](#ref-World-on_populate) works on
the engine's overworld (`world: overworld`, or `mode: full` with no `world`
key). It gets each new chunk with terrain, caves and ores in place, with the
same `chunk:get`, `chunk:set` and `chunk:fill` as `on_generate`. Use it for
your own ores and trees. Like `on_generate` it is a single-handler setter, and
a changed hook reaches new land only.

## The chunk API

A chunk is a 16 by 16 column of blocks, handed to `world.on_generate`,
`world.on_populate` and a room's `generate` to fill. Fields: `chunk.x` and
`chunk.z` are the chunk coordinates (16 blocks each); `chunk.min` is the
chunk's lowest corner, inclusive (y runs 0..255 or the game version's height),
and `chunk.max` the highest, inclusive.

| Call | Returns | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`chunk:get(pos: Vec3)`](#ref-Chunk-get) | `string` | The block there now, by name; air outside the chunk |
| [`chunk:set(pos: Vec3, block: string)`](#ref-Chunk-set) | — | Sets one block; positions outside the chunk are ignored |
| [`chunk:fill(from: Vec3, to: Vec3, block: string)`](#ref-Chunk-fill) | — | Fills a box of blocks, clipped to the chunk |
| [`chunk:paste(schem, origin, opts?)`](#ref-Chunk-paste) | — | Pastes a build or schematic, clipped to this chunk |
| [`chunk:get_biome(pos: Vec3)`](#ref-Chunk-get_biome) | `string?` | The biome of the column at `pos`; `nil` outside the chunk |
| [`chunk:set_biome(pos: Vec3, biome: string)`](#ref-Chunk-set_biome) | — | Sets one column's biome: a vanilla name or a `game.biomes.define` name |
| [`chunk:fill_biome(from: Vec3, to: Vec3, biome: string)`](#ref-Chunk-fill_biome) | — | Sets the biome of every column in a box, clipped |

`chunk:paste` takes the same `{ air = true, part = "name" }` options as
[`world.paste`](#ref-World-paste): `part` names the paste for
`citadel render --part` and `citadel check`, and the build's own `b:part`s are
then inside it (`"house/roof"`).

> **Note:**
> a read never generates — a position in an unloaded chunk reads as
> `nil` (not loaded), not `"air"`. Inside `on_generate`, `chunk:get` always
> works.


## Making generation fast

Everything a chunk needs should be made once, at the top of the script, not
inside the generator:

- Make each **noise** at the top of the script, and ask for a chunk with one
  `grid` call — 256 `get` calls are slower.
- Make **builds** at the top of the script, and paste one per chunk.
  `world.schematic` inside `on_generate` reads the file again for every chunk.
- The engine calculates noise, so a generator stays inside its 100 ms.

## Noise

`noise` gives smooth random numbers for hills, caves and biome borders. The
same seed gives the same numbers every time.

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `seed` | 0 | the same seed gives the same numbers each time |
| `scale` | 64 | the size of one hill, in blocks |
| `octaves` | 1 | layers of detail, 1 to 16 |
| `lacunarity` | 2 | how many times finer each next layer is |
| `gain` | 0.5 | how many times as strong each next layer is |

A world with hills and two biomes:

```luau
local hills = noise.new { seed = 7, scale = 96, octaves = 4 }
local climate = noise.new { seed = 8, scale = 300 }

world.on_generate(function(chunk)
    local h = hills:grid(chunk.min.x, chunk.min.z, 16, 16)
    local c = climate:grid(chunk.min.x, chunk.min.z, 16, 16)
    for z = 0, 15 do
        for x = 0, 15 do
            local i = z * 16 + x + 1
            local at = chunk.min + vec3(x, 0, z)
            local top = 64 + math.floor(h[i] * 24)
            local dry = c[i] > 0
            chunk:fill(at, at + vec3(0, top - 1, 0), "stone")
            chunk:set(at + vec3(0, top, 0), dry and "sand" or "grass_block")
            chunk:set_biome(at, dry and "desert" or "forest")
        end
    end
end)
```

> **Tip:**
> `grid` gives up to 65 536 numbers (256 x 256), row by row: the
> number for `(x + dx, z + dz)` is at `[dz * width + dx + 1]`.


<a id="world-terrain-generation--biomes"></a>

## Biomes

A biome is what the client colours a column by: the grass, the leaves, the
water, the sky and the fog. It is also the weather there. Each block column has
one biome.

- A column that nothing sets is `"plains"`.
- The engine's overworld sets the biomes of its own chunks. `on_populate` can
  read them and change them.
- A name is a vanilla biome name of any release: `"windswept_hills"` and
  `"mountains"` are the same hill. A wrong name is an error.
- A client that lacks a biome shows the nearest one it has. A 1.8 client shows
  `"cherry_grove"` as plains.

A pack makes biomes of its own. A new biome is a copy of a vanilla biome with
other colours and weather:

```luau
local crystal = game.biomes.define {
    name = "crystal",        -- becomes "mypack:crystal", which define returns
    like = "forest",         -- the vanilla biome to copy; "plains" when left out
    grass = "#7fd8c8",       -- each colour is a colour name or a color value
    leaves = "#58b7a6",
    water = "#3fd0ff",
    water_fog = "#0a4060",   -- the view under water
    sky = "#b0e8ff",
    fog = "#e0f6ff",         -- the far distance
    weather = "snow",        -- "rain" or "snow"; "none" or false for no weather
}

world.on_generate(function(chunk)
    chunk:fill_biome(chunk.min, chunk.max, crystal)
end)
```

- Define biomes at the top of the script. A client learns the biomes when it
  joins.
- Clients from 1.16.2 show a new biome. An older client and a Bedrock client
  show the `like` biome.
- A changed colour reaches a player on the next join. A biome that is new after
  the first player joined shows as its `like` until the server restarts. The
  console says so.
- A colour that is left out stays as `like` has it. `weather = "snow"` also
  makes the grass and leaves colder in colour, unless you set them.
- A biome does not make trees or blocks. The generator puts them there.

<a id="world-terrain-generation--the-a010-terrain-steps"></a>

## The a0.1.0 terrain steps

`terrain` in citadel.yml sets the overworld's step list. Only
`game: a0.1.0` has one; `terrain` on a 1.8.9 world stops the server. Without
`terrain`, the world uses the original game's steps.

```yaml
game: a0.1.0
world: overworld
terrain:
  snow: true              # Alpha's snowy world: a frozen sea, snow on every open column
  steps:                  # the whole populate list, in order, in place of the jar's
    - { step: dungeons, count: 8 }
    - { step: clay, block: clay, size: 32, count: 10 }
    - { step: ore, block: coal_ore, size: 16, count: 20, below: 128 }
    - { step: ore, block: diamond_ore, size: 7, count: 4, below: 16 }   # four times the jar's
    - { step: trees, bonus: 10, big: 10 }
    - { step: patch, block: dandelion, count: 2 }
    - { step: patch, block: poppy, count: 1, chance: 2 }
    - { step: reeds, count: 10 }
    - { step: cactus, count: 1 }
    - { step: springs, fluid: water, count: 50, bound: 120, nesting: 1 }
    - { step: springs, fluid: lava, count: 20, bound: 112, nesting: 2 }
    - { step: snow }
```

| step | what it places |
| --- | --- |
| `dungeons` | `count` tries at a cobblestone room with a spawner and up to two chests |
| `clay` | `count` blobs of `block`, `size` long, into sand that starts under water |
| `ore` | `count` veins of `block`, `size` long, into stone below y `below` |
| `trees` | trees on the surface; one chunk in `bonus` gets one more, one in `big` grows big trees |
| `patch` | a patch of 64 tries at `block` — `count` times, or with `chance: n` one time in n |
| `reeds` | `count` clumps of sugar cane beside water |
| `cactus` | `count` clumps of cactus on sand |
| `springs` | `count` fluid sources in stone walls; `nesting` pushes them deeper |
| `snow` | a snow layer on every open column — in a `snow: true` world only |

> **Gotcha:**
> order matters — moving or removing a step changes everything
> after it. A block must be one the game can name, a size or a bound must be at
> least 1, and an unknown key stops the server. The list is stored in
> `level.json`; like `seed`, a later edit changes nothing for an existing
> world.


[`game.terrain`](#ref-Game-terrain) prints the original list — start an edit
from it. Its rows are the `step`, `block` and `count` of each step (see
[Game data](#world-game-data)).

## A declared world

[`world.generate(rules: GeneratorRules) → Generated`](#ref-World-generate)
declares a world as rules. The engine makes each chunk from them, on all cores,
and no script runs for a chunk. Use it for a large world; `world.on_generate`
stays for what the rules cannot say.

```luau
local hills = fields.noise { seed = 7, scale = 96, octaves = 4 }
local dry = fields.noise { seed = 8, scale = 300 }:gt(0)

local made = world.generate {
    height = 64 + hills * 24,                -- the y of the surface
    sea = 62,                                -- water fills the open air up to here
    biomes = { { "desert", when = dry }, { "forest" } },   -- the first that holds
    surface = {                              -- the first rule that holds, for each block
        { block = "stone", when = fields.slope:gt(2), depth = 4 },
        { block = "sand", biome = "desert", depth = 4 },
        { block = "grass_block" },           -- depth 1: the top block
        { block = "dirt", depth = 4 },       -- the 3 blocks below it
    },
    rock = { { block = "stone" } },          -- the body of the land
    plants = { { block = "short_grass", chance = 0.3, biome = "forest" } },
    things = { { cell = 8, { shapes = { oak }, chance = 0.4, biome = "forest" } } },
}
made:sample(hills, pos)     -- a field's value there, as the engine calculates it
made:biome_at(pos)          -- "forest"
```

### Fields

A **field** is a number at each block, written as a recipe. `fields.noise` gives
one, and maths on fields gives more: `+ - * / ^`, a minus sign, and the
methods. A number is a field too.

```luau
-- 1 on a column with water beside it: sugar cane beside water.
local w = fields.water
local beside_water = w:at(1, 0, 0):max(w:at(-1, 0, 0)):max(w:at(0, 0, 1)):max(w:at(0, 0, -1)):gt(0.5)
plants = { { block = "sugar_cane", height = 2, chance = 0.5, when = beside_water * w:lt(0.5) } }
```

- A rule asks a question with `when`: it holds where the field is above 0.5.
  `a * b` is "and", `a:max(b)` is "or", `1 - a` is "not".
- `height` cannot use `fields.height`, `slope`, `water` or `shore`: they are
  read from it.
- `biome` in a rule is a biome name. It is the same as a `when`, and faster.

### The rules

| Key | A rule | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `biomes` | `{ "desert", when = f }` | the first that holds names the biome of the column |
| `surface` | `{ block, biome, when, depth }` | `block` for the top `depth` blocks (1) of each surface |
| `rock` | the same | the body of the land under the surface rules |
| `plants` | `{ block, chance, biome, when, ... }` | at most one plant on a column |
| `things` | `{ cell, seed, { shapes, chance, biome, when, afloat, place, y }, ... }` | at most one thing in a grid cell |
| `fluids` | `{ block, below, biome, when }` | the carved air under `below` becomes `block`; the first that holds |

`sea` fills the open air with water up to its y, and `floor` is the block at
y 0 (`"bedrock"` for a land of its own).

- A **block** is a name, or a list with a field that chooses:
  `{ "stone", "andesite", by = fields.hash(3) * 2 }`. `floor(by)` counts
  through the list.
- A **plant** is `block`, or `blocks = { lower, upper }` for a plant of two
  blocks. With `height = f` it grows: `block` repeats, and `tip` is the top
  block. `afloat = true` puts it on the water, and `sink = 1` puts it one block
  lower (ice in the top of the sea). `clear = n` keeps `n` blocks of water free
  over a plant that grows in water.
- A column tries the plant rules in order. Each rule that holds takes its
  `chance` of the column's roll, so two rules of 0.3 and 0.2 give a plant on
  half of the columns.
- A plant stays only where the game version's own rule lets it stay, for
  example cane needs water beside the block under it, at the same level. Where
  the rule fails, the column has no plant. Light is not known yet, so a rule
  about light is not checked.
- A **thing** is one of `shapes`: builds from `world.build` or
  `world.schematic`. Its `(0, 0, 0)` goes on the block above the ground. A
  thing that crosses a chunk border is complete. Nothing stands on ground that
  is under water, but `afloat = true` puts the thing on the water.
- `density = f` makes a block solid where `f` is above 0. Use it with a `solid`
  noise for caves, overhangs and land in the air. With `height` too, a block
  must pass both.
- Without `height` and `density`, the rules add to the land that the engine's
  own terrain made (`world: overworld`): surface rules do not run, plants grow
  on each column, and a thing must stand inside one chunk.
- Make the shapes and the fields at the top of the script, within the load
  limits.

### Caves

`density` carves air under the top surface. A plant or a thing goes into that
air with `place`, and `fluids` fill it:

```luau
local caves = fields.noise { seed = 3, scale = 24, octaves = 2, solid = true }
world.generate {
    height = 72 + hills * 20,
    density = 1 - caves:abs():lt(0.12) * fields.y:gt(5),   -- caves under y 5 and up
    rock = { { block = "stone" } },
    plants = {
        { block = "moss_carpet", place = "floor", chance = 0.6 },          -- moss on cave floors
        { block = "cave_vines_plant", tip = "cave_vines", height = fields.room / 3,
          place = "ceiling", chance = 0.3 },                               -- glow berries from the ceilings
        { block = "glow_lichen[{wall}=true]", place = "wall", chance = 0.1, y = { 0, 50 } },
    },
    fluids = { { block = "water", below = 30 }, { block = "lava", below = 10 } },  -- a lake, and lava under it
    things = { { cell = 6, { shapes = { stalagmite }, place = "floor", when = fields.room:gt(5) } } },
}
```

| `place` | Where | At most |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"top"` (the default) | on the top surface, as before | one plant on a column |
| `"floor"` | the air block over each floor of a cave | one plant on each floor |
| `"ceiling"` | the air block under each ceiling, hanging down | one plant under each ceiling |
| `"wall"` | each air block of a cave with rock on a side (plants only) | one plant in each block |

- A column can cross many caves. Each floor and each ceiling of each cave is
  its own place, with its own roll.
- `y = { low, high }` keeps a rule to the blocks it starts at from `low` to
  `high`. `when`, `chance` and `y` are read at the air block the plant starts
  in, not at the rock under it.
- A plant that grows (`height`) under a ceiling hangs down: `block` is at the
  ceiling and `tip` is the lowest block. With `blocks`, the first is at the
  ceiling. A plant never grows into rock, a fluid or another plant.
- A wall plant is one block. In its name, `{wall}` is the side the rock is on
  and `{facing}` is the side away from it: `"vine[{wall}=true]"`,
  `"wall_torch[facing={facing}]"`, `"cocoa[facing={wall}]"`.
- A thing on a floor has its `(0, 0, 0)` on the air block over the floor. A
  thing under a ceiling has its `(0, 0, 0)` on the air block under the ceiling,
  so build it down from there (negative y). A grid cell holds one thing; when
  its column has several caves, the cell's roll picks one. A thing does not
  look at fluids or at the size of the cave: use `when = fields.room:gt(n)` and
  `y` to keep it in a cave it fits.
- A fluid fills only carved air, from the floor of a cave up to `below - 1`.
  The open sky over the top surface is the `sea`'s, not the fluids'. A cave
  that opens to the sea from the side is not flooded: give it a fluid rule
  under the sea level. Plants go only where the air stays air.
- `fields.room` counts the air block, the air over it and the air under it, up
  to 64. The open sky over the top surface reads 64. Read it with `at`
  anywhere; another column's room costs one `density` read for each block of
  it. `density` cannot use `fields.room`.
- `fields.depth` is measured from `height`, so it needs a `height`.
- The game version's own plant rule holds in caves too. On 1.8.9, grass and
  flowers need dirt under them, so a stone floor keeps none. Cave blocks that
  1.8.9 does not have (moss, glow lichen, hanging roots, cave vines) stay.
  `vine` keeps its 1.8.9 rule: rock on its side.

> **Gotcha:**
> caves need `density` or `carvers` — a rule with `place` under the
> top, or a fluid, without one of them is an error.


### The game's own caves and structures

`carvers` and `structures` run the game version's own generators over the
declared land, with the world seed:

```luau
world.generate {
    height = 64 + hills * 20,
    rock = { { block = "stone" } },
    carvers = { "caves", "ravines" },        -- the game's tunnels and ravines
    structures = { "mineshaft", "dungeon" }, -- with rails, spawners and loot
    plants = { { block = "moss_carpet", place = "floor" } },  -- in those caves
}
```

| Key | Names | Versions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `carvers` | `"caves"` | every version |
|  | `"ravines"` | b1.8 and later |
| `structures` | `"mineshaft"`, `"dungeon"` | 1.7 to 1.12 |

- They dig and build after the land (`height`, `density`) and before the
  plants, fluids and things, so the cave rules (`place`, `fluids`) use the
  caves they dig. They need `height` or `density`: the game's own terrain
  (`world: overworld`) has its own.
- A dungeon's spawner has its mob and its chest has its loot, as in the game.
  Without the lists, the world has none of them.
- A name this version does not have is an error that names the ones it has.

## See also

- [Block reference](#world-block-reference) — block names, `[property=value]`
  states, version fallbacks, and how reads behave.
- [Building](#world-building) — `world.build` values pasted per chunk, and
  `.schem` files.
- [Game data](#world-game-data) — `game.terrain` and the per-version registry.
- [Server settings](#systems-server-settings) — citadel.yml: `game`, `world_dir`,
  `seed`, and where the world lives.
- [Runtime](#concepts-runtime) — the tick budget, and the separate 2 s chunk
  callback limit.
- [Rooms and dimensions](#concepts-rooms-and-dimensions) — other worlds and their
  own `world` tables.

<!-- /world/block-reference/ -->

<a id="world-block-reference"></a>

## Block reference

> **In short:**
> how a block is named, written, read and substituted. Names are
> Minecraft's canonical names without `minecraft:`; properties go in brackets
> in any order and any subset; every version's blocks are real and stored
> exactly, with nearest-block fallbacks in both directions. Plus the two
> special cases: player heads with skins, and the `detail = 2` half-block
> system inside builds.


## Names

Block names are Minecraft's, without `minecraft:`.

- Every block of every version is real here and stored exactly. An older client
  sees the nearest block its version has.
- Properties go in brackets, in any order and any subset:
  `"oak_trapdoor[facing=east]"`, `"stone_button[facing=west, face=wall]"`.
  Missing properties come from the default state. The nearest state wins.
- A name that is no block of any version (`"grassblock"`, `"stone_brick"`) is
  an error that lists the nearest real names.
- Queries ([`game.block(name)`](#ref-Game-block), the block an entity stands
  on) return `nil` for a name the game lacks.

A block from [`game.blocks.define`](#ref-Blocks-define) works wherever a name
works — its handle or its namespaced name (`"rave:crate"`). See
[Custom blocks](#world-custom-blocks).

## Version fallbacks

| Situation | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| A name this game version lacks | the nearest block it has — never air |
| An older client than the block | the client sees the nearest block its version has |
| A name no version has (`"grassblock"`) | an error that lists the nearest real names |

- A block name may list `|` alternatives (`"deepslate|stone"`): the first one
  the game version knows wins. Write `"future_block|obsidian"` to pick the
  substitute yourself. Without `|`, an unknown name becomes the nearest block,
  never air.

## Writing blocks

| Call | Returns | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`world.set_block(pos, block, opts?)`](#ref-World-set_block) | — | Sets one block, live, stored and sent |
| [`world.set_blocks(changes)`](#ref-World-set_blocks) | — | Sets many blocks at once; the cheapest way |
| [`world.fill(from, to, block)`](#ref-World-fill) | — | Fills a box between two corners, live, stored and sent to everyone |

`block` is a `BlockRef`: a name string or a custom-block handle. Both
`set_block` and `set_blocks` take `skin` for player heads — a row of
`set_blocks` is `{ at = ..., block = ..., skin = ... }`.

## Reading blocks

**A read never generates.** A position in an unloaded chunk reads as `nil`
(not loaded), not `"air"`. Inside `on_generate`, `chunk:get` always works. A
block change is stored, so late joiners see it.

| Call | Returns | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`world.get_block(pos)`](#ref-World-get_block) | `string?` | The block's name; `nil` where the chunk is not in memory |
| [`world.get_blocks(from, to)`](#ref-World-get_blocks) | `{string?}` | A box of names, in x, then z, then y order |
| [`world.block(pos)`](#ref-World-block) | `BlockAt?` | The block there as the handle a hook gets |
| [`world.light_at(pos)`](#ref-World-light_at) | `number, number, boolean` | Block light and sky light, 0 to 15, and whether nothing above holds off the sky |
| [`world.get_biome(pos)`](#ref-World-get_biome) | `string?` | The biome name of the column; `nil` where not in memory |

`world.block` gives the live handle every block hook receives:

- Reads are the world as it is now; what it does lands on the next tick, like
  `world.set_block`.
- Fields read (`at`, `name` with its namespace, `room`); methods act:
  [`block:get(face)`](#ref-BlockAt-get), [`block:set(block)`](#ref-BlockAt-set),
  [`block:destroy()`](#ref-BlockAt-destroy), `block:become(entity, data)`,
  `block:drop(item, count?)`, `block:schedule()`, `block:notify()`.
- `block.state` and `block.data` are for blocks this pack defined. On any other
  block they are an error.
- A handle you keep does nothing once its block is gone.

## Player heads

A `"player_head"` or `"player_wall_head"` shows a face when you give it a
`skin`:

```luau
world.set_block(vec3(0, 65, 0), "player_head[rotation=8]", { skin = "Notch" })
world.set_block(vec3(1, 65, 0), "player_wall_head[facing=south]", { skin = player.name })
world.set_block(vec3(2, 65, 0), "player_head", { skin = { value = "ewogICJ0aW1l...", signature = "..." } })
world.set_blocks({ { at = vec3(3, 65, 0), block = "player_head", skin = "jeb_" } })
```

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| a name string | looked up from a player in this room, else from Mojang |
| `{ value = , signature = }` | the account's `textures` property; the signature is optional |

- The head appears at once and gets its face later. A name with no account
  leaves a plain head and logs a line.
- The `{ value = , signature = }` form is the account's `textures` property, as
  for `world.npc{ skin = }`.
- The face is saved with the chunk. Replacing, breaking or turning the head
  forgets it: write the new state with its `skin` again.
- A head in a `.schem` (Sponge or MCEdit) or an imported world keeps its face
  through pastes, turns and `citadel import`. A head saved with only a name is
  looked up when its chunk loads.
- `skin` on any other block is an error.
- Clients from 1.7 see the face. Bedrock clients see no face.

For a head as an **item** — a face in a hand, a hotbar slot, a menu — see
[Inventory](#players-inventory).

<a id="world-block-reference--half-blocks-detail--2"></a>

## Half blocks: `detail = 2`

At `detail = 2` in [`world.build`](#ref-World-build), every coordinate is a
half block. The engine turns each block's eight cells into the block, a slab or
a stair of the material, with the correct `facing`, `half` and `shape`:

```luau
local roof = world.build(function(b)
    for k = 0, 9 do                          -- a 45-degree roof, half a block a step
        b:box(vec3(k, k, 0), vec3(19 - k, k, 15), "deepslate_tiles")
    end
end, { detail = 2 })                         -- 10 blocks wide: coordinates 0..19
```

| cells of a block | what is placed |
| --- | --- |
| all eight | the block |
| the bottom four, or the top four | a bottom or top slab |
| a half and one quarter above it (or below) | an outer-corner stair |
| a half and two quarters on one side | a straight stair, climbing that side |
| a half and three quarters | an inner-corner stair |
| anything else | the block when four or more cells hold it, else nothing |

- The slab and the stair are the material's own: `stone_bricks` makes
  `stone_brick_slab` and `stone_brick_stairs`, `oak_planks` makes `oak_slab`,
  `quartz_block` makes `quartz_stairs`.
- A material with no slab or stairs, or whose slab or stairs came in a later
  release (concrete's), is the whole block or nothing.
- Only full blocks are fitted. A lantern, flower, fence or stair named directly
  is placed as named in a block with no full-block cells. So a detail is one
  `b:block`, not eight.
- A block that holds two materials takes the one most of its cells hold.
- `detail` is `1` (the default) or `2`. `build.size` and `build.min` are in
  blocks. The cube limit counts cells, so detail 2 holds an eighth as many
  blocks.

## What a block does on its own

[`game.block(name)`](#ref-Game-block) returns one block in **this version's**
numbers, or `nil` if this game lacks it. Its `behaviour` field is the rule
Citadel runs for the block — `"grass"`, `"flowing"`, `"torch"` or `"falling"` —
or `nil` for an inert block. `resistance`, `flammability` and `material` are
`nil`, not zero, in a game with no block-update tables. Everything is
read-only. The full field table is in [Game data](#world-game-data).

## See also

- [Terrain generation](#world-terrain-generation) — chunk reads inside
  `on_generate`, biomes, and the declared world.
- [Custom blocks](#world-custom-blocks) — `game.blocks.define`, the block
  handle, `state` and `data`.
- [Game data](#world-game-data) — `game.block(name)` fields and block
  behaviour rules.
- [Building](#world-building) — `world.build`, where `detail = 2` fits slabs and
  stairs.
- [Client versions](#appendix-client-versions) — which clients see which
  blocks and features.

<!-- /world/building/ -->

<a id="world-building"></a>

## Building

> **In short:**
> a build a script writes is a schematic with no file — write it
> with `world.build`, turn it, crop it, paste it, or read a `.schem` from the
> pack. This page covers the Builder API and the Schematic value, the size
> budget, `.schem` import, the `citadel render` / `citadel check` workflow, how
> to build well, and named parts with their generators and build mode.


## A build is a schematic with no file

```luau
local road = world.build(function(b)
    b:box(vec3(-4, 0, -48), vec3(4, 0, 48), "gray_concrete")
    b:line(vec3(0, 0, -48), vec3(0, 0, 48), "white_concrete")
    b:block(vec3(0, 1, 0), "sea_lantern")     -- later writes win
end)
road.size, road.min          -- vec3(9, 2, 97) and vec3(-4, 0, -48)
world.paste(road, vec3(0, 64, 0))             -- road.min lands here
```

The rules:

- Coordinates are whole blocks in the build's own space, and may be negative. A
  build written around `vec3(0, 0, 0)` lands with its middle `-build.min` from
  `origin`.
- A block name this game version lacks becomes the nearest block it has.
- `chunk:paste` and `world.paste` take a build like any schematic. Make it at
  the top of the script, not inside `on_generate`.
- A build costs only what it writes. One build may write 4 096 16-block cubes
  (32 MB, sixteen million solid blocks), in a box of up to 256 million blocks.
  For more, use several builds or a `.schem`.
- Fences, walls, glass panes and iron bars join their neighbours, and stairs
  take their corners. Write `"oak_fence"`, not its `north=true` states.

## The Builder

What [`world.build`](#ref-World-build) hands the function it is given.
Coordinates are whole blocks of the build's own and may be negative; later
writes win. `{ detail = 2 }` makes every coordinate a half block, fitted to
slabs and stairs — see [Block reference](#world-block-reference--half-blocks-detail--2).

| Call | Returns | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`b:block(pos, block)`](#ref-Builder-block) | — | Sets one block of the build; later writes win |
| [`b:box(from, to, block)`](#ref-Builder-box) | — | Inclusive corners, in any order, like `chunk:fill` |
| [`b:line(from, to, block)`](#ref-Builder-line) | — | Every block the straight line between the ends passes through |
| [`b:part(name, fn)`](#ref-Builder-part) | — | What `fn` writes is a named part; nested calls name `"tower/roof"` |

### Naming the parts inside a build

A build names its pieces as it writes them, and the names stay after the paste.
`citadel render` frames a part by name. `citadel check` says which part an edit
touched.

```luau
local house = world.build(function(b)
    b:part("walls", function()
        b:box(vec3(-5, 0, -4), vec3(5, 4, 4), "stone_bricks")
        b:part("door", function() ... end)      -- "walls/door"
    end)
    b:part("roof", function() ... end)
end, { detail = 2 })
world.paste(house, vec3(0, 64, 0), { part = "house" })   -- "house", "house/walls", "house/roof"
chunk:paste(house, vec3(0, 64, 0), { part = "house" })   -- the same from on_generate
```

- A part is the box its writes reached, in whole blocks at either detail. It
  turns and flips with the build.
- A name is 1 to 64 characters without a `/`. A part inside another part is
  named by its path, `"walls/door"`.
- A name may repeat. Selecting it takes every part with that name.
- Name the parts you will talk about: the body, each tower or wing, the roof,
  the entrance. Then "make the tower taller" stays an edit to the tower.

## Schematic values

A build is a [`Schematic`](#ref-Schematic): a box of blocks, like a `.schem`
file read once by `world.schematic`. `size` is the build's width, height and
length in blocks; `min` is the build's own lowest corner, which is the corner
`origin` puts down — zero for a file.

| Call | Returns | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`world.paste(schem, origin, opts?)`](#ref-World-paste) | — | Live, stored and sent; air is skipped unless `air = true` |
| [`schematic:rotate(degrees)`](#ref-Schematic-rotate) | `Schematic` | A new build turned clockwise seen from above |
| [`schematic:mirror(axis)`](#ref-Schematic-mirror) | `Schematic` | A new build flipped: `"x"` swaps east and west, `"z"` north and south |

<a id="world-building--turning-a-build"></a>

## Turning a build

A build turns and flips as a value; the original does not change.

- A build turns about `vec3(0, 0, 0)`, so a part drawn around its middle turns
  in place. `min` reads back the new start.
- Block states turn with it: facings, log axes, fence and pane sides, stair
  corners, door hinges, rail curves, sign and banner rotation.
- `rotate` takes 90, 180 or 270. Any other value is an error.

## Cutting a build, and changing its blocks

A build somebody made by hand is a kit of pieces. `crop` takes one piece out of
it, and `replace` makes it of other blocks. Both give a new build; the original
does not change.

- The corners are in the build's own blocks, in either order. A file's lowest
  corner is `vec3(0, 0, 0)`.
- A box that reaches outside the build is cut to it. A box with none of the
  build in it is an error that says where the build runs.
- A cropped piece has no named parts. `replace` keeps them.
- `replace` takes block names with no state. A block keeps its state where the
  new block has one like it: stairs stay stairs that face the same way. Where
  it has none, the block is the plain block. `"air"` takes a block away.
- A name that is not a block is an error that names it.
- To save memory, crop the pieces while the pack loads and keep only them: a
  file nobody holds is let go.

## `.schem` files

Ship a build too big for `chunk:set` lines as a `.schem` in the pack folder,
and paste it:

```luau
local lobby = world.schematic("builds/lobby.schem")   -- at the top, not per chunk
world.on_generate(function(chunk)
    chunk:paste(lobby, vec3(0, 64, 0))         -- origin is the build's lowest corner
end)
world.paste(lobby, vec3(100, 64, 0))           -- the same build, live
chunk:paste(lobby, vec3(0, 64, 0), { air = true })   -- both take this third argument
```

The rules:

- `file` is a path inside the pack folder, written with `/`. These are errors
  that name the file: a path from the root, a path that leaves the pack with
  `..`, a missing file, and a file that is not a schematic.
- Call [`world.schematic`](#ref-World-schematic) while the pack loads and keep
  the value. Inside `on_generate`, it reads the file again for every chunk.
- `origin` is where the build's **lowest** corner goes. The build fills `origin`
  to `origin + schem.size - vec3(1, 1, 1)`.
- Air in the build is skipped, so a paste sits on the terrain. Pass
  `{ air = true }` to place the air too.
- `chunk:paste` writes only the part inside its chunk, so the call in
  `on_generate` builds the whole thing. `world.paste` writes all of it at once,
  like `world.set_blocks`.
- Sponge v2, Sponge v3 and the old MCEdit `.schematic` all load. Block
  entities (chest contents, signs) and entities do not: a chest pastes empty.
- A paste does not turn. Turn the value first with `:rotate` or `:mirror` (see
  [turning a build](#world-building--turning-a-build)). A file's schematic has them too.
- A paste keeps the exact blocks of any release Citadel knows. A newer name
  becomes the nearest block. What nothing covers becomes air, and the log names
  and counts it once per file.

## Building well

**Plan before code.** Write the plan as a comment at the top of the build:

1. What makes it recognisable at a glance? A keep is tall, square and crowned;
   a market is low and crowded.
2. Its parts, each with bounds, material and joins: footing, body, openings,
   roof, trim, props.
3. Its setting: neighbours, ground, and the way a player approaches.
4. Where detail goes: the skyline, doors, windows, corners, the roof line,
   places a player stops.

**Build in that order, and look at each stage before the next.** End each stage
with a render and a check. Name the parts as you go (`b:part`), so renders and
the check can name them.

| stage | what is built | look with | ask |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. massing | the footprint, the main volumes, the roof shapes | `--view sides,roof` | Does the outline say what it is? Are the proportions right: towers tall enough, roof steep enough, wings in scale? |
| 2. architecture | openings, wall depth, eaves, how parts join | `--view approach,entrance,plan` and `citadel check` | Are windows holes with sills and frames? Does the way in read? Can a player walk to every floor? |
| 3. setting and detail | paths, ground, lighting, props, trim | `--view approach,cutaway` and `citadel check` | Does it sit in a place? Is the detail where the eye goes? |

At each stage:

- Write down the three worst problems the pictures and the check show.
- Fix those, then look again with the same views.
- Finish every fix before the next stage.
- Render again only after a change or for a new question.

**The four ways a build fails:**

- *Painted flat.* A window keeps its glass in the wall's plane, with a sill and
  a frame that stand out in front of it; glass pushed behind a wall one block
  thick sits inside the room. Give walls depth: plinths, beams, cornices.
- *Visible boxes.* Taper what grows: a tower narrows, a roof flares at its
  eaves. Break long edges. Let parts overlap and sink into each other.
- *No setting.* Add a path, a fence, a tree, a barrel, a lamp, and shape the
  ground to meet them.
- *Detail everywhere, or nowhere.* Put detail where the eye goes.

**Half blocks are the detail.** Use `detail = 2` for shapes finer than a block:
roofs, eaves, sills, steps, cornices, arches. The build turns half steps into
stairs and slabs. Name `oak_fence` or `glass_pane` and the build joins them.

**Conventions that keep a build square.**

- An axis of symmetry runs through a block's middle, so a symmetric thing is
  odd: a door 1 or 3 wide, a gate 5, a path 3. `build:mirror("x")` of one half
  gives the other.
- A block is inside a circle when `math.sqrt(dx * dx + dz * dz) <= r + 0.5`.
  The `+ 0.5` gives flat edges.
- Mix a large surface from two or three blocks of one family, chosen by a hash
  of the position. A restart then builds the same wall.
- Write a part once, round its own middle. Place it with `build:rotate` and
  `build:mirror`.

```luau
-- Helpers a pack writes for itself; nothing here is the engine's.
local function hash(x, y, z)                         -- 0..1, the same every time
    local v = math.sin(x * 12.9898 + y * 4.1414 + z * 78.233) * 43758.5453
    return v - math.floor(v)
end
local function mix(x, y, z, blocks)                  -- { "stone_bricks", "stone_bricks", "cracked_stone_bricks" }
    return blocks[math.floor(hash(x, y, z) * #blocks) + 1]
end
local function disc(b, at, r, block)                 -- 2r + 1 across, round the block `at`
    for dx = -r, r do
        for dz = -r, r do
            if math.sqrt(dx * dx + dz * dz) <= r + 0.5 then
                b:block(at + vec3(dx, 0, dz), block)
            end
        end
    end
end
local function cone(b, at, r, height, block)         -- a tower roof, widest at `at`
    for y = 0, height do
        local rr = r * (1 - y / (height + 1))
        for dx = -r, r do
            for dz = -r, r do
                if math.sqrt(dx * dx + dz * dz) <= rr + 0.5 then
                    b:block(at + vec3(dx, y, dz), block)
                end
            end
        end
    end
end
```

**Look at it, and say what you saw.** Only `citadel render` and
`citadel check` prove a build good.

- Judge only pictures taken after the last edit.
- Fix every `fix` from `citadel check`, or say it is deliberate. Weigh advice
  against the build's purpose, and say what you chose.
- After an edit to one part, run `citadel check --since` to show the other
  parts did not change.
- The pictures are flat colour. Report textures as unchecked.
- Report what you looked at, what you fixed, and what is left.

## Seeing what you built

`citadel render <pack dir> --out view.png` runs the pack with nobody joining
and draws its world.

- Each block has its real shape, in the average colour of its textures.
- With named parts, four cameras frame them from the sides (`view-1.png` looks
  north). Otherwise they circle the spawn.

Ask for the view that answers your question:

```sh
citadel render ./castle --out v.png --view approach,entrance     # does the way in read?
citadel render ./castle --out v.png --view roof --part castle/keep
citadel render ./castle --out v.png --view plan,cutaway          # the enclosed spaces, storey by storey
citadel render ./castle --out gate.png --at 0,66,30 --look 0,70,-10   # one camera, placed
```

| view | camera | the question it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sides` | four, round the build, a little above it | silhouette and proportion from every side |
| `approach` | a player's eye height, out from the main door | what a player sees walking up to it |
| `entrance` | close on the main door, eye height | does the way in read as the way in |
| `roof` | high up, at an angle | the roof line, and where the parts meet |
| `plan` | straight down, to scale, one per storey | the enclosed spaces, walls and doors of each floor |
| `cutaway` | at an angle, one per storey | the enclosed spaces as a player stands in them |
| `eye` | in each named part, where a player stands, at eye height | the part as one who walks in sees it: a hall from inside, a square from its edge |
| `night` | as `sides`, at night | the light: only blocks that give light (lanterns, lamps, glowstone, froglights) light the build |

- `--part name` frames that part and the parts inside it.
  `--from x,y,z --to x,y,z` frames a box. Without either, `--view` frames every
  named part.
- The main door is the lowest door that opens outdoors. A build with no
  `*_door` block has no `approach` or `entrance` view.
- `plan` and `cutaway` remove everything above each storey. `--cut y` removes
  everything above `y` for any view. `--night` draws any view at night, the
  placed cameras of `--at` too.
- Under a roof, a face is lit by the sky light that comes in through the
  openings and by the light blocks near it, as in the game: a room with windows
  is light, one without is dark.
- `--around x,y,z`, `--distance d`, `--height h` and `--views n` circle a point
  instead. `--size 1280x720`, `--fov 60` and `--radius r` (how far around the
  target the world is read) change the rest.
- Each file prints one JSON line on stdout:
  `{"file":..., "view":..., "eye":[x,y,z], "look":[x,y,z]}`, with `"cut"` when
  something was removed.

> **Note:**
> a picture proves shape, depth, proportion and silhouette, not
> textures: every block is one flat colour. Say so when you report on how a
> build looks. At night a block is lit by the light blocks within 15 blocks of
> it, as in the game; a lamp outside the views' box lights nothing.


## Checking what you built

`citadel check <pack dir>` measures the named build and reports what is wrong
with it:

```sh
citadel check ./castle                          # every named part
citadel check ./castle --part castle/keep --storeys 3 --enclosed
citadel check ./castle --save before.snap       # write the blocks down ...
citadel check ./castle --since before.snap      # ... and say what changed, part by part
```

It lists:

- the enclosed spaces (the air closed in with doors and windows shut)
- how many blocks the build holds
- the storeys
- for each innermost part: its places to stand and the detail near them (blocks
  within reach that are not a full cube and not glass)
- the doors, and where each opens
- each face: how much is one plane, its windows and how many are framed, its
  materials
- the roof: how much is one height, how much is stairs and slabs
- the setting: how much of the ground around it has something placed

Then it lists the findings:

| finding | kind | what it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FLOATING` | fix | blocks that touch nothing standing |
| `DOOR_BLOCKED` | fix | a block in a door's way at foot or head height, named |
| `DOOR_DROP` | fix | a door that opens onto nothing to stand on |
| `DOOR_UNREACHED` | fix | a door nobody can walk to from outside |
| `UNREACHED` | fix | floor inside walls and under a roof that nobody can walk to from outside |
| `STOREYS` | fix | `--storeys n` asked for, and not what enclosed spaces stand on |
| `NOT_CLOSED_IN` | fix with `--enclosed` | outside air reaches the inside with doors and windows shut, and where it comes in |
| `FLAT_FACE` | advice | a face nearly all in one plane |
| `FLUSH_WINDOWS` | advice | windows with nothing in front of them: no sill, lintel or post that stands out |
| `ONE_MATERIAL` | advice | a face nearly all one block |
| `FLAT_ROOF` | advice | the top one flat height, not stepped |
| `BLOCKY_ROOF` | advice | a sloping roof of whole blocks where stairs could be |
| `LOW_CEILING` | advice | a room two blocks high |
| `NO_SETTING` | advice | bare ground all round |
| `BARE_FACE` | advice | a face with few shape blocks (stairs, slabs, walls, trapdoors, lanterns): masses without detail |
| `DARK_AT_NIGHT` | advice | over half of the places a player walks to is dark at night |
| `SPARSE` | advice | a part where players walk with little detail near them: an empty hall, square or deck |
| `PART_OVERLAP` | advice | two parts (`parts.define`) overlap without one inside the other: regenerating either rewrites the other |

- A fix is wrong for any build. Weigh advice against the build's purpose: a
  market stall is open, and a tower's roof may be flat.
- A player walks on two clear cells over something solid, steps onto stairs and
  slabs, jumps one block, drops three, and climbs ladders and vines. Blocks are
  sorted by their names.
- `--json` prints one JSON object. The command exits 1 when there is something
  to fix.
- `--since` counts changed blocks by the innermost part that holds them, and
  counts the rest as `(in no part)`.

<a id="world-building--named-parts"></a>

## Named parts

`parts.define` declares a part of a stored world and the generator that writes
it — for builds you edit by hand and regenerate from code:

```luau
parts.define {
    name = "tower-3",                  -- unique; a path, "downtown/tower-3", nests
    at = vec3(56, 64, 15),             -- where the build's block (0, 0, 0) lands
    detail = 1,                        -- as world.build: 1, or 2 for half blocks
    build = function(b) ... end,       -- exactly a world.build function
}
```

The rules:

- **Nothing runs on load.** `parts.define` only declares the part. A generator
  runs on request (`citadel generate`, or `/part generate` in build mode) or
  when its code changes. A server boots the stored world and runs no generator.
- Each word of a name is 1 to 64 letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`.
- A duplicate name is an error that names the file of the first definition.
- A part is its whole box, air included. Writing it again clears what the old
  box held outside the new box.
- `citadel render` and `citadel check` frame the `b:part`s inside a part by
  path, for example `"tower-3/roof"`.
- On a `world: script` pack, `parts.define` logs that parts need a world
  folder, and generates nothing.

### Part states

Each part is in one of four states, kept in `<world>/parts.json`:

| state | means | when its code changes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **clean** | the box holds exactly what its generator last wrote | written again, by itself |
| **modified** | somebody edited blocks in it since | left alone, and reported: "its code changed" |
| **kept** | somebody chose its blocks: they are in `parts/<name>.schem` in the pack | ignored: the generator no longer owns it |
| **orphaned** | its definition is gone from the pack | reported: keep it, or regenerate it to remove its blocks |

```json
{ "tower-3": {
    "state": "modified",
    "region": [[48, 64, 4], [64, 119, 26]],
    "module": "city.luau",
    "generated": "sha256:…",
    "at": "2026-09-27T14:02:11Z",
    "edits": { "count": 214, "by": { "melvin": 200, "agent:claude": 14 } }
} }
```

**Only people and the agent make edits, never scripts.**

- An edit in build mode counts under the player's name. An agent edit counts
  under `agent:<client>`.
- Either kind makes a clean part modified.
- Blocks your script writes are not edits: `world.set_block` from a callback, a
  door it opens, a display, a ride.
- `citadel parts` and `/part` confirm the state against the `generated` hash. A
  modified part with every edit undone is clean again.

**You regenerate or keep a whole part.** Hand edits never merge into new code.

- `regenerate` clears the part and runs its generator. On an orphan, it removes
  the blocks.
- `keep` saves the blocks to `parts/<name>.schem` as Sponge v3, the format
  `world.schematic` reads. Generating a kept part pastes that file.
- `release` deletes the file and regenerates the part.

**When the code changes.** Saving a `.luau` file reloads the pack. Parts defined
**in that file** then act as the table says.

- A clean part is written again through the tick. Unchanged blocks are skipped.
- On start, files changed while the server was down count too.
- A change to a module that a part `require`s re-runs nothing.

**Nested and overlapping parts.** A block belongs to the innermost part whose
box holds it.

- Writing a parent leaves its nested parts alone.
- An edit inside a nested part counts against it, not its parent.
- Where parts overlap without nesting, an edit counts against each.
  `citadel check` warns (`PART_OVERLAP`): regenerating one rewrites the other.

### The `citadel` commands

From the command line, on the world folder:

```sh
citadel generate <pack> --part tower-3      # run one generator into the world; --parts runs every one
citadel parts <pack>                        # every part: state, region, module, edits and who; --json
citadel regenerate <pack> --part tower-3 [--yes] [--render before.png]
citadel keep <pack> --part tower-3          # its blocks become parts/tower-3.schem
citadel release <pack> --part tower-3       # a kept part goes back to its generator
```

- `generate` makes the world folder if it is missing. It writes new and clean
  parts, pastes kept parts from their files, and refuses modified parts.
- `regenerate` of a part with hand edits needs `--yes`. Without it, it writes
  nothing and says how many blocks of whose edits it would overwrite.
- `--render file.png` writes `file-before.png` and `file-after.png`.
- Stop any server running the pack first, or use `/part` in the game.
- `citadel check` and `citadel render` read the world folder with its hand
  edits. The check report has a "part states" section: states, edits, authors,
  and code changes.

### Build mode

Build mode works only on a development copy (`citadel.env` is `"development"`),
never on a live instance. A player with the `citadel.build` permission builds
by hand. Every operator has it.

```
/build                          creative and flight, and your clicks change the world; again to stop
/build wand                     the wooden axe: left click the first corner, right click the second
/build pos1, /build pos2        a corner where you stand
/build fill <block>             the selection, filled
/build replace <from> <to>      one block for another in the selection
/build copy                     the selection, held from where you stand
/build paste                    the clipboard, the same way round you as it was copied
/build rotate <90|180|270>      the clipboard, turned about where you stood
/build mirror <x|z>             the clipboard, flipped
/build undo                     your last edit, taken back
/part                           the part you look at: its state, its region, who edited it
/part <name>, /part list        one part by name; every part
/part generate <name>           run a part's generator
/part regenerate [name] [confirm]   throw its hand edits away; asks for "confirm" when there are some
/part keep [name]               its blocks become parts/<name>.schem
/part release [name]            a kept part back to its generator
/part outline                   every part's box nearby, 15 seconds: green clean, amber modified, blue kept, red orphaned
```

- Every block a builder changes, undo included, is an edit under their name.
- Outside build mode, a click on a pack server changes no blocks.
- A place puts the held item's block, facing as in the game. A pack's own block
  item places the pack's block.
- Undo is per player, 64 edits deep. One command is one edit of at most one
  million blocks.
- Rotate and mirror turn facings, axes and shapes, as `build:rotate` and
  `build:mirror` do.
- The outline is particles for the asking player only, on clients from 1.7.

## See also

- [Terrain generation](#world-terrain-generation) — pasting builds per chunk
  inside `on_generate`, and `world.generate` for whole worlds.
- [Block reference](#world-block-reference) — block names, states and the
  `detail = 2` cells table.
- [Custom blocks](#world-custom-blocks) — `game.blocks.define` blocks placed in
  builds and by hand.
- [Build a cottage](#guides-guide-build-a-cottage) — the full walkthrough of
  plan, parts, render and check.
- [Server settings](#systems-server-settings) — `world: hub` folders,
  `citadel generate` over a range, and where the world lives.
- [Tooling](#getting-started-tooling) — the `citadel` CLI commands at a glance.

<!-- /world/custom-blocks/ -->

<a id="world-custom-blocks"></a>

## Custom blocks

> **In short:**
> `game.blocks.define` makes a block of your pack's own — a real
> block, saved under its own name, broken, used and ticked like any other, that
> clients which have never heard of your pack draw as its `looks` block. This
> page covers the definition fields, states and `block.data`, the hook system
> with `base`, drops, redstone power, and blocks with their own pictures and
> models on 1.21.4 and later.


## Defining a block

```luau
local crate = game.blocks.define {
    name = "crate",
    looks = "tnt",
    on_use = function(block, player)
        block:become("primed_tnt", { fuse = 20 })
        return "used"
    end,
}

world.set_block(vec3(10, 65, 10), crate)   -- the handle, or "rave:crate"
```

It is a real block: saved under its own name, broken, used and ticked like any
other. Every client that has never heard of your pack draws it as TNT. Three
rules apply:

- **The engine adds the namespace.** `"crate"` becomes `"rave:crate"`, after
  your pack. A colon in the name is an error. The handle `define` returns works
  wherever a block name works.
- **`looks` is all a client sees.** Pick an inert block state that reads right.
  A name this version lacks is an error, not air. `|` takes the first name that
  exists: `looks = "crimson_planks|nether_brick"`.
- **Hooks record changes; the engine applies them.** `block:become` takes
  effect when your hook returns.

## The definition

```luau
game.blocks.define {
    name = "crate",              -- no namespace: yours is added
    looks = "tnt",               -- or { "wheat[age=0]", "wheat[age=7]" }, one per state
    hardness = 0.5,              -- seconds-scale; below zero is unbreakable
    resistance = 6,              -- what an explosion has to chew through
    material = { solid = true, covers = false, firm = true, liquid = false, burns = false },
    opacity = 15,                -- what a step through it takes off the light
    light = 0,                   -- what it gives off, 0..15
    tick_every = 0.5,            -- seconds between block:schedule() and on_tick
    drops = { { item = "stick", count = 2 } },   -- or "table"; "none" or false for nothing; a row may be a pack item
    item = { item = "furnace", name = "Crate" },  -- the block in a hand; see "the block as an item"; false for no item
    texture = "textures/crate.png",  -- its own picture on 1.21.4+; see "blocks with their own pictures"
    model = models.crate,        -- or its own shape, in place of texture; see "blocks drawn from a model"
    facing = true,               -- turns its front to whoever places it
    power = 0,                   -- what it gives a redstone circuit, 0 or 15; see "power"
    label = "Crate",             -- the name of the item a textured block comes with
    extends = "tnt",             -- a name, a handle, a plain table, or a list
    on_use = function(block, player, held, base) end,
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | no namespace: yours is added |
| `looks` | one block state, or a list with one per state |
| `hardness` | seconds-scale; below zero is unbreakable |
| `resistance` | what an explosion has to chew through |
| `material` | `{ solid, covers, firm, liquid, burns }` |
| `opacity` | what a step through it takes off the light |
| `light` | what it gives off, 0..15 |
| `tick_every` | seconds between `block:schedule()` and `on_tick` |
| `drops` | a drops list, or `"table"`; `"none"` or `false` for nothing; a row may be a pack item |
| `item` | the block in a hand; `false` for no item |
| `texture` | its own picture on 1.21.4+, in place of the `looks` cube |
| `model` | its own shape, in place of `texture` |
| `facing` | turns its front to whoever places it |
| `power` | what it gives a redstone circuit, 0 or 15 |
| `label` | the name of the item a textured block comes with |
| `extends` | a name, a handle, a plain table, or a list |

- Every field except `name` and `looks` has a default.
- Call `define` only **while your pack loads**. Define blocks at the top of
  `main.luau`. A reload runs `define` again and keeps the world.

The handle `define` returns is a [`BlockDef`](#ref-BlockDef): `name` (canonical,
with the pack's namespace already on it: `"rave:crate"`), `states` (how many
states it has; `block.state` counts 1 to this) and `item` (the block as an
item, when the definition gave it one: `player:give(def.item)`).

## States and the block handle

For crop stages, give one `looks` per stage and write `block.state = 3`. The
value must be in that list. A state change keeps the block: `block.data` stays,
and `on_removed` and `on_added` are not called.

Every hook gets the block it is about. Fields read; methods act:

| Member | Kind | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `block.at` | field | The block's position; a live read |
| `block.name` | field | The name with its namespace, such as `"rave:crate"` |
| `block.room` | field | Which room the block is in |
| `block.state` | field | Which of this definition's states it is in, counting from 1; writable, bounds-checked |
| `block.facing` | field | A facing block's front: `"north"`, `"south"`, `"west"`, `"east"`; writable |
| `block.powered` | field | Whether a redstone signal reaches it; nil where the chunk is not loaded |
| `block.data` | field | What this block remembers beyond its state (see below) |
| [`block:get(face)`](#ref-BlockAt-get) | method | The block one face away, by name |
| [`block:set(block)`](#ref-BlockAt-set) | method | Puts another block at this position |
| [`block:destroy()`](#ref-BlockAt-destroy) | method | Takes it out, leaving nothing |
| `block:become(entity, data?)` | method | This block stops being a block, and that entity appears |
| `block:drop(item, count?)` | method | A name, or an item table: a pack item keeps its id |
| `block:schedule()` | method | Asks for this block's `on_tick`, `tick_every` seconds from now |
| `block:notify()` | method | Tells the six neighbours this block changed |

[`world.block(pos)`](#ref-World-block) is the same handle, for any block: reads
are the world as it is now, and what it does lands on the next tick, like
`world.set_block`. `block.state` and `block.data` are for blocks this pack
defined — on any other block they are an error. A handle you keep does nothing
once its block is gone.

## `block.data`

`block.data` holds what a block remembers besides its state, such as a chest's
contents. It is a [data view](#world-custom-blocks--data-views): nested edits and whole-record
assignments are tracked, just like a pack-defined entity's `data`. Read and
write its fields:

```luau
on_use = function(block, player)
    block.data.clicks = (block.data.clicks or 0) + 1
    player:message(`clicked {block.data.clicks} times`)
    return "used"
end,
```

- `block.data` belongs to the **position**. It saves with the chunk, through
  reloads and restarts.
- Each write is checked at the assignment by the `storage.set` rules. A bad
  value is an error that names the key.
- When the block goes, its data goes.
- Pack-wide facts, such as a leaderboard, go in `storage`.

<a id="world-custom-blocks--data-views"></a>

## Data views

`block.data` and a pack-defined entity's `data` are attached records. Nested
records and lists are attached too: `e.data.stats.wins += 1` writes back without
assigning the whole record again. This works on handles from `world.spawn` and
`world.entities`, as well as handles passed to hooks.

```luau
e.data = { stats = { wins = 0 }, history = {} }
local stats = e.data.stats
stats.wins += 1
data.insert(e.data.history, { score = 12 })
e.data.history[1].score += 3
local last = data.remove(e.data.history) -- removes and returns a detached value
local snapshot = data.copy(e.data)      -- an ordinary, detached Lua table
snapshot.stats.wins = 99               -- does not change the entity
```

- Roots are records with string keys. Values can be finite numbers, strings,
  booleans, records, or contiguous lists starting at index 1. Functions, handles,
  cycles, sparse lists, and tables mixing list indices and record keys raise an
  error before any part of that assignment changes the record.
- Set a record field to `nil` to delete it. Write `list[#list + 1] = value` to
  append, or use `data.insert(list, value)` / `data.insert(list, index, value)`.
  `data.remove(list, index?)` shifts following elements; its default is the last
  element. Assigning `nil` only removes the last list element. An empty nested
  `{}` becomes a list on the first insertion; the root always stays a record.
- `#view` counts entries. Use `for key, value in view do` to iterate. Data views
  are userdata, so use `data.copy(view)` before ordinary `table.*`, `pairs`, or
  `ipairs` operations. `storage.set(key, view)` accepts views directly.
- A nested alias follows its path in the current record. Replacing that path
  with another record or list updates what the alias sees. Deleting it or
  replacing it with a scalar makes the alias raise an error.
- Entity `on_steer`/`on_tick` and block hooks edit a draft applied when the
  engine accepts the hook's answer. Their views expire when the callback batch
  finishes, including on error. Use `data.copy` inside the hook to keep a
  snapshot, or obtain a current entity handle to edit later. Live entity views
  remain valid while the entity exists. An unchanged draft does not overwrite
  entity data.
- `player.data` remains an ordinary Lua table for the player's session. It can
  hold Lua objects such as HUD handles; it is not saved automatically.
  Persistent entity data saves only with `persist = "save"`; block data saves
  with its chunk.

> **Note:**
> migration — direct and nested assignments now write through on
> every supported handle. Replace table operations on persistent data with the
> `data` helpers or operate on `data.copy(...)` and assign the result back.
> Mutating the Lua table originally assigned to a record does not mutate the
> stored record.


## The hooks

Every hook gets the block first and `base` last:

| hook | called when | arguments | answers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `on_use` | somebody right-clicked it | `block, player, held, base` | `"used"` or `"pass"` |
| `on_break` | something broke it | `block, player, by, base` | `"none"`, `"table"`, or a drops list |
| `on_step` | a body is standing on it | `block, body, base` | nothing |
| `on_tick` | a scheduled tick came due | `block, base` | nothing |
| `on_random_tick` | the random pass landed on it | `block, base` | nothing |
| `on_place` | a player put it down | `block, player, base` | nothing |
| `on_neighbour` | a neighbour changed | `block, from, announced, base` | nothing |
| `on_trigger` | lit, blasted or burnt | `block, cause, base` | nothing |
| `on_power` | a redstone signal started or stopped reaching it | `block, powered, base` | nothing |
| `on_added` | it has just been stored, whatever stored it | `block, base` | nothing |
| `on_removed` | it has just gone | `block, base` | nothing |

- `player` is a handle. It is `nil` for a break with no player, or once that
  player left.
- `held` is the item in hand.
- `by` is `{ cause = "player" | "fire" | "explosion" | "water" | "support",
  tool, creative }`.
- `body` is `{ id, kind = "player" | "mob" | "item" | "other" }`. `body.kind`
  is `"mob"` for a cow or a zombie.
- `cause` is `"ignite"`, `"explosion"` or `"fire"`. A redstone signal is not a
  cause: it has `on_power`.
- `powered` is `true` when the signal started and `false` when it stopped.
- `from` is a `vec3`. `announced` is the name the notifying block gave.

> **Gotcha:**
> a hook exists only if you write it. There is no flag such as
> `random_ticks = true`. A block with no `on_step` is never asked about steps.


**Hooks answer with words, never booleans.** `"used"` takes the click; `"pass"`
does not. `"none"` leaves nothing. `"table"` leaves what the breaker would
normally leave. An answer nothing reads is an error that names it.

## Extends, and `base`

`extends` takes a handle, a game block's name, a plain table, or a list of
those, **innermost first**. Data fields merge; hooks *wrap*.

```luau
-- A mixin is only a table.
local glowing = { light = 12 }
game.blocks.define { name = "lamp", looks = "gold_block", extends = glowing }

-- A crate that is a tnt underneath.
game.blocks.define {
    name = "bomb",
    looks = "tnt",
    extends = "tnt",
    drops = { { item = "stick", count = 1 } },
    on_break = function(block, player, by, base)
        base(block, player, by)    -- a0.1.0 lights every tnt a player digs
        return "none"              -- ...but this one leaves what *we* said
    end,
}
```

Every hook takes **`base` as its last argument**. Call it to extend the block
underneath; leave it out to replace it. Its effects land when your hook returns,
and a second call counts once.

Two rules for merging:

- **A game block's data is the floor**, wherever it is in the list.
  `extends = "tnt"` gives tnt's hardness and blast resistance unless you or a
  mixin set them. Your values beat inherited ones.
- **A hook you do not write is not asked.** The block underneath answers it.
  Extending tnt with no hooks costs nothing, even while your pack sleeps.

## Amending the game's own

```luau
game.blocks.amend("tnt", {
    on_break = function(block, player, by, base)
        player:message("careful")
        base(block, player, by)
    end,
})
```

- **Hooks only.** A data field is an error that names it. For different numbers,
  use `game.blocks.define { extends = "tnt" }`.
- **Only the game's own blocks.** Never another pack's.

## What a missed deadline means, per hook

Each hook has a deadline. This is what a miss means:

| hook | a missed deadline means | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `on_use` | **the click passes through** (`"pass"`) | fail-open. A busy pack must not stop people using the rest of the world, and a click that did nothing is visible where a click that was silently eaten is not. |
| `on_break` | **the block leaves the drops its definition declared** — never the looks block's | fail-**closed**. `drops = "table"` on a crate that looks like TNT would drop TNT, and anything that makes items must never make them twice. A definition that declared nothing leaves nothing. |
| `on_step`, `on_tick`, `on_random_tick`, `on_place`, `on_neighbour`, `on_trigger`, `on_power`, `on_added`, `on_removed` | **the block did not react this tick** | fail-open, and it costs nothing: the engine had already decided what it was doing. These are batched — five hundred crops taking their random tick are one message under one deadline — and answered at the end of the tick that asked. |

`can_stay`, `can_place_at` and `power` are **not** pack hooks. A pack block
answers them from its definition's data and what it extends: `power` is a
field, below.

## Power

A block gives a redstone circuit power, hears one, or both. A script flips it
from anywhere with `world.block(pos)`:

```luau
-- A card reader: a click gives power for two seconds.
game.blocks.define {
    name = "reader",
    looks = { "iron_block", "redstone_block" },
    power = { 0, 15 },                    -- one value per state
    tick_every = 2,
    on_use = function(block) block.state = 2  block:schedule()  return "used" end,
    on_tick = function(block) block.state = 1 end,
}

-- A receiver: something happens when a wire reaches it.
game.blocks.define {
    name = "receiver",
    looks = "note_block",
    on_power = function(block, powered)
        if powered then sound.play("block.note_block.pling", { at = block.at }) end
    end,
}

local door = world.block(vec3(10, 65, 10))   -- the block there, or nil where the chunk is not loaded
if door and door.powered then print(door.name, "has a signal") end
world.block(vec3(4, 65, 4)).state = 2        -- a timer, a command or a zone turns the reader there on
```

`power` says what a state gives:

- A number is every face: `power = 15`. A list is one value per state, like
  `looks`.
- A table keyed by face gives it on those faces only, with the names `texture`
  takes: `power = { top = 15 }`, `power = { 0, { front = 15 } }`. `front` and
  `back` need `facing = true`.
- A value is 0 or 15. The game's signal has one strength, and a wire fades it
  by itself. Any other number is an error.
- It is the power a block of redstone gives: it lights the wire, lamp or piston
  that touches the face, and does not pass through a solid block.
- A state change that changes the power tells the neighbours. There is no
  `block:notify()` to remember.
- Without `power`, a block gives what it extends gives: `extends = "lever"`.
- Before 1.13 the client draws a wire's shape itself, from the `looks` block. A
  wire only bends toward a block that looks like a redstone part.

`on_power` says when the signal changed:

- It is called once when a signal starts to reach the block and once when it
  stops, not for every change beside it. `block.powered` reads it at any time,
  in any hook.
- The signal is the one a lamp reacts to: a lever or a lit wire beside the
  block, or a powered solid block next to it. The block's own power counts when
  it comes back through a wire.
- The last answer is saved with the block, so a restart repeats nothing. For a
  block of the game (`game.blocks.amend`) it is kept in memory: after a restart
  the first change beside it reports the signal as it is.
- A block of the game that becomes another block when it is powered is two
  blocks: `redstone_lamp` and `lit_redstone_lamp`.
- A pack's part reacts at the end of the tick, so it is a tick behind the
  game's own. For exact timing, extend a repeater.

> **Gotcha:**
> `world.rules{ redstone = false }` stops every signal in a room —
> see [World state](#world-world-state--redstone).


## Blocks with their own pictures

`texture` gives a block its own picture on 1.21.4 and later. `facing = true`
turns its front to whoever places it, like a furnace:

```luau
local side = game.texture(16, 16)
side:noise(0, 0, 16, 16, { "#8a8a8a", "#7d7d7d", "#969696" }, 3)
side:frame(0, 0, 16, 16, "#5a5a5a")
local front = side:copy()
front:rect(4, 4, 8, 8, "#303030")

local macerator = game.blocks.define {
    name = "macerator",
    looks = "dispenser",                  -- what an older client sees; left out, stone
    texture = { side = side, top = side, bottom = side, front = front },
    facing = true,
    label = "Macerator",                  -- the item's name
}
player:give(macerator.item)
```

- `texture` is one picture for all six faces, or a table of `all`, `side`,
  `top`, `bottom`, `front`, `back`, or a face by name (`north`, `up`, …).
  `front` is the side a facing block faces; `back` is opposite. A missing face
  uses `side`, and `side` uses `all`.
- Several states take a list, one per state:
  `texture = { idle, working }` with `looks = { "furnace", "furnace[lit=true]" }`.
- `facing = true` gives every state four facings. `block.state` counts only
  your states. `block.facing` reads and turns the facing (`"north"`,
  `"south"`, `"west"`, `"east"`). The `looks` block turns too if it can.
- A textured block comes with its item. `label` names it. `item` sets another
  item underneath. `item = false` gives the block no item.
- The picture is a full, opaque cube: see-through pixels draw solid. A server
  has room for about a thousand textured blocks.
- A client from 1.21.4 draws a textured cube on a note block state, so it hears
  a note block (wood) when the block is hit or broken. An older client hears
  the `looks` block.
- A block a pack places is never drawn as a textured block. A pale moss carpet
  with moss up its sides can show as a bare one.
- The block collides as its `looks` block does. One that looks like a rail or a
  carpet is drawn on a state a client walks through or over; a server has room
  for about a hundred of each. See
  [blocks drawn from a model](#world-custom-blocks--blocks-drawn-from-a-model).

<a id="world-custom-blocks--blocks-drawn-from-a-model"></a>

## Blocks drawn from a model

`model` draws a block from a model on 1.21.4 and later, in place of `texture`.
This is a conveyor belt whose top runs by itself:

```luau
local belt = models.new("belt", function(m)
    local frame = m:material("frame", colors.gray, { grain = 0.2 })
    local strip = m:texture(16, 16, { scroll = "up", speed = 2 })   -- two texels a tick, on the client
    strip:fill(colors.black)
    strip:rect(0, 0, 16, 2, colors.gray)
    m:part("body"):box(vec3(-8, 0, -8), vec3(8, 16, 8), frame, { faces = { up = strip } })
end)

local DIR = { north = vec3(0, 0, -1), south = vec3(0, 0, 1), west = vec3(-1, 0, 0), east = vec3(1, 0, 0) }

game.blocks.define {
    name = "belt",
    looks = "stone",                      -- what an older client sees; left out, stone
    model = belt,
    facing = true,
    label = "Conveyor Belt",
    on_step = function(block, body)       -- carry what lies on it toward the block's front
        if body.kind ~= "item" then return end
        local at, dir = block.at, DIR[block.facing]
        for _, it in world.entities { near = vec3(at.x + 0.5, at.y + 1, at.z + 0.5), radius = 1.5 } do
            if it.id == body.id then it:push(vec3(dir.x * 0.05, 0, dir.z * 0.05)) end
        end
    end,
}
```

- The model stays inside its block: `-8 .. 8` across and `0 .. 16` up. A box
  outside that is an error. A bigger shape is a display.
- **A block collides as its `looks` block does**, for the server and for every
  client. `looks` picks what the model is drawn on:
  - A full cube (`"stone"`, the default): players stand on it, and the client
    does not draw the sides of its neighbours that touch it. Where the model
    leaves the side of the cube open, you see through the neighbour. Fill the
    block's sides.
  - A block you walk through (`"rail"`, `"stone_pressure_plate"`): the model
    can be any low shape, and nothing around it is hidden. A stack dropped on
    it lies on the block below, and `on_step` still hears it. A client from
    1.21.4 breaks it at a touch, whatever its `hardness`; a `hardness` below
    zero still cannot be broken.
  - A carpet (`"white_carpet"`): a sixteenth of a block high.
  - Any other shape (a slab, a fence) is drawn on a full cube.
- A low belt is the same definition with `looks = "rail"` and a model two units
  high. It needs a floor under it. Give it `opacity = 0`, or the block is dark
  inside.
- A block draws the model in its rest pose. It plays no animation and takes no
  `paint`. A see-through material draws solid.
- A texture with `scroll` moves by itself on the client, with nothing sent:
  `"up"`, `"down"`, `"left"` or `"right"`, at `speed` texels a tick. A speed is
  a whole number, or `0.5`, `0.25`, `0.2` for one texel every few ticks. On a
  top face, `"up"` runs toward the model's front (`-z`), which is where
  `block.facing` points. A display draws a scrolling texture still.
- `model` is one model for every state, or a list with one per state, like
  `texture`. `texture` and `model` together are an error.
- Like a textured block, it comes with its item, and it uses one spare state
  per state and facing.

## The block as an item

`item` is the block in a hand, with the block's name as its `id`. Placing it
puts **this** block down. Breaking the block leaves it, unless `drops` says
otherwise:

```luau
local macerator = game.blocks.define {
    name = "macerator", looks = "furnace",
    item = { item = "furnace", name = "Macerator", lore = { "grinds ore into dust" } },
}
player:give(macerator.item)       -- a Macerator; place it and it is one
game.recipes.shaped{ pattern = { "FFF", "F F", "FFF" }, keys = { F = "flint" }, result = macerator.item }
```

Placing it fires `players.on_place`, then the block's `on_place` with the placer
and an empty `block.data`.

## See also

- [Block reference](#world-block-reference) — block names, states, version
  fallbacks, and `world.block` reads.
- [World state](#world-world-state) — the `redstone` rule that stops every
  signal in a room.
- [Game data](#world-game-data) — `game.block(name)` and the game's own blocks.
- [Custom entities](#entities-custom-entities) — entity `data` uses the same data
  views as `block.data`.
- [Displays](#ui-displays) — models that stand in the world, animate and take
  `paint`.
