<!-- /world/game-data/ -->

<a id="world-game-data"></a>

## Game data

> **In short:**
> `game` reads the game version a room runs: one block in this
> version's numbers with `game.block(name)`, items with `game.item(name)`,
> entity kinds with `game.entities.<kind>`, and the overworld's terrain list
> with `game.terrain`. The one field a pack writes on the game's own things is
> the tri-state `spawn`, `attacks`, `interact` and block `drops` — `true`,
> `false` or `nil`.


## `game.block(name)`

[`game.block(name)`](#ref-Game-block) returns one block in **this version's**
numbers, or `nil` if this game lacks it.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `string` | The block's canonical name |
| `behaviour` | `string?` | The rule Citadel runs for it: `"grass"`, `"flowing"`, `"torch"` or `"falling"`; `nil` for a block that does nothing on its own |
| `hardness` | `number` | Seconds-scale hardness in this version's numbers; below zero is unbreakable |
| `random_ticks` | `boolean` | Whether the random-tick pass acts on it |
| `opaque` | `boolean` | Whether it is an opaque full cube, which is not the material's question |
| `light` | `number` | What it gives off, 0..15, and what a step through it takes away |
| `light_filter` | `number` | What a step through it takes off the light, 0 to 15 |
| `resistance` | `number?` | The three the block-update tables own: `nil` in a game that has none |
| `flammability` | `{ catches: number, burns_away: number }?` | Fire's two numbers: how readily it catches and how fast it burns away |
| `material` | `Material?` | The jar's Material as five questions; `nil` in a game with no block-update tables |
| `drops` | `boolean?` | The one field a pack writes — see below |

`resistance`, `flammability` and `material` are `nil`, not zero, in a game with
no block-update tables. Everything above is read-only.

### `drops` — `true`, `false` and `nil`

`drops` is the field of a game block that a pack writes. It says whether a
block of this kind leaves its item when the world breaks it by itself: a torch
whose wall is gone, a leaf that decays, a block an explosion or a piston
breaks, sand that cannot land. On a `mode: lite` world, the world leaves no
such item. The pack switches a block on:

| Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `true` | The world leaves the block's normal drops, on a lite world too. |
| `false` | The world leaves nothing for this block, with `survival` on too. |
| `nil` | The pack sets nothing. The world's default applies. |

- The world's default is off on a `mode: lite` world and in a room made by
  `rooms.create`. It is on on a `mode: full` world and after
  `world.rules{ survival = true }`.
- The value is for every state of the block, and for this block name only.
  `oak_planks` and `spruce_planks` are two blocks.
- It reads what this pack set, not another pack's value. Where two packs
  disagree, `false` wins.
- It is not a player's dig. Without `survival`, a dig reaches no block.
- Use it for the game's blocks. A block from `game.blocks.define` leaves the
  drops its definition lists.
- A reload removes a value that the script does not set again.
- `true` is an error in a game version with no items on the ground.

## `game.item(name)`

[`game.item(name)`](#ref-Game-item) does the same for items: the item's table,
or `nil`. It never raises an error.

## Entity kinds

A kind is a `mob` when the game gives it health and a mind of its own: a cow, a
zombie. An arrow, an item and a boat are not mobs. A player is not an entity
here: players are in `players`, never in `world.entities`.

`game.entities.<kind>` has the facts of one kind of the game.
`game.entities.cow` and `game.entities.Cow` are the same kind. A kind that this
game does not have is `nil`: `if game.entities.creeper then`.

```luau
local cow = game.entities.cow
print(cow.max_health, cow.width, cow.height, cow.speed)   -- cow.health is an error: a kind has a maximum
print(cow.drop)                      -- "leather"
print(cow.hostile)                   -- false
print(cow.registry_name)             -- "Cow", this version's own spelling
print(cow.mob)                    -- true: a cow is a mob

for name, kind in game.entities do   -- every mob kind this version has, in its own order
    if kind.hostile then print(name) end
end

local arrow = game.entities.arrow    -- a kind that is not a mob has a row too
print(arrow.mob)                  -- false
print(arrow.width, arrow.height, arrow.physics)

game.entities.names()                    -- every kind: the pack's own and the game's, mob or not
game.entities.names { mob = true }    -- the mob kinds only
game.entities.names { mob = false }   -- the kinds that are not mobs
```

| Fact | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | Its modern registry name: `"cow"` |
| `mob` | Whether the kind is a mob: `true` for a cow, `false` for an arrow |
| `max_health` | The most health one of this kind has, in this version's numbers. `health` on a kind is an error: health is what one entity has now |
| `width`, `height` | Its size in blocks, in this version's numbers |
| `speed` | Blocks a tick at a full walk |
| `hostile` | Whether it is hostile |
| `drop` | The item its death leaves behind, such as `"leather"`; `nil` for none |
| `registry_name` | This version's own registry spelling: `"Cow"`. A dungeon spawner stores this one |
| `physics` | For a kind that is not a mob, which order of operations moves it: `"item"`, `"falling"`, `"vehicle"` or `"none"`. `nil` for a mob kind |
| `behaviour` | The name of the behaviour the engine runs for this kind, such as `"sheep"` or `"living"` |
| `profile` | Read-only copy; `nil` for a specialized behaviour without a shared profile |

- Use `for name, kind in game.entities do`, not `pairs(game.entities)`.
- A game kind that is not a mob (an arrow, a boat, primed TNT) has the facts
  `name`, `mob` (`false`), `width`, `height` and `physics`. Every other fact is
  `nil`. A write to `spawn`, `attacks` or `interact` is an error, and so is
  `:amend`: they are for mob kinds.
- Iteration and `game.entities.names()` cover all kinds, once each. Use
  `game.entities.names { mob = true }` or check `kind.mob` for mob settings.
- A pack kind (`rave:rocket`) reads as a definition handle, with `name` and
  `mob = false`. Pass it to `world.spawn` just like the handle from `define`.
- `define`, `amend` and `names` are functions on the same table (see
  [Custom entities](#entities-custom-entities)). `game.entities.cow:amend { ... }`
  is the same as `game.entities.amend("cow", { ... })`.

Everything above is read-only.

## `spawn` — `true`, `false` and `nil`

`spawn` is the field of a mob kind that a pack writes. It says whether the kind
is in this world by itself. On a `mode: lite` world, no mob spawns by itself;
the pack switches a kind on, and it then spawns by the game's own rule.

| Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `true` | The kind is in this world as the game defines it. It spawns by the game's own rule, and it is the game's entity in full. |
| `false` | The kind never spawns by itself. |
| `nil` | The pack sets nothing. The world's default applies. |

- The world's default is off on a `mode: lite` world and in a room made by
  `rooms.create`: no mob spawns by itself. The default is on on a `mode: full`
  world and after `world.rules{ survival = true }`: each kind spawns by the
  game's own rule. `world.rules{ survival = false }` sets the default to off
  again.
- `true` makes the kind the game's entity in full, on a lite world too. It
  spawns by the game's own rule. Its hits hurt players and a player's right
  click on it has the game's effect. See
  [`attacks` and `interact`](#world-game-data--attacks-and-interact).
- A monster that comes to a sleeping player obeys the same value.
- `true` does not make a kind spawn where the game cannot spawn it. On 1.8.9
  the game takes the kinds it spawns from the biome. A world with no biomes (a
  world the scripts make) spawns nothing, and `true` is an error there.
- `false` stops natural spawning only. A spawner block, `world.spawn`,
  `/summon` and breeding still make the entity.
- Mobs already in the world stay.
- Reading gives what this pack set: `true`, `false` or `nil`. It does not give
  the game's own rule or the value of a different pack.
- Each pack has its own value. If one pack sets `false`, the kind does not
  spawn. If no pack sets `false` and one pack sets `true`, the kind is on.
- The value is for one room. `game` is the main room's table. A room from
  `rooms.create` has its own: `room.game.entities.cow.spawn = true`.
- On a script reload, the values of the last run stay until the new script has
  loaded. Then each value that the new script did not set is removed.
- On a game with no natural spawning, every write is an error, `nil` included.
  a0.1.0 to a0.1.3 are such games.
- An error is a plain string for `pcall`.

<a id="world-game-data--attacks-and-interact"></a>

## `attacks` and `interact`

`attacks` and `interact` are two more fields of a mob kind that a pack writes.
Each is `true`, `false` or `nil`. A different value is an error.

| Field | `true` | `false` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `attacks` | The entity's hits hurt players. | The entity's hits do not hurt players. |
| `interact` | A player's right click on the entity has the game's effect (milk from a cow, a saddle on a pig). | The right click has no effect. |

With `nil`, the engine uses the first line that applies:

1. The kind has `spawn = true`: the field is on.
2. The room's rule: `damage` for `attacks`, `survival` for `interact`.

- **The kind's own setting is stronger than the room's rule.** Thus
  `game.entities.zombie.spawn = true` makes a zombie's hit hurt in a room with
  `world.rules{ damage = false }`. To keep the zombie harmless there, set
  `game.entities.zombie.attacks = false`.
- A zombie from `world.spawn` on a lite world does not hurt players until the
  pack sets `spawn = true` or `attacks = true` for zombies, or the room has the
  `damage` rule.
- `interact` changes the item in the player's hand as the game does: an empty
  bucket becomes a bucket of milk.
- `interact` is not available on 1.8.9: that game version has no right click on
  a mob in Citadel. `interact = true` is an error there, and `spawn = true`
  does not give the right click.
- `attacks` covers the entity's own hit, its arrow and its blast. An arrow
  keeps the kind of its shooter, so the arrow of a dead skeleton follows
  `game.entities.skeleton.attacks`. The blast of a creeper follows
  `game.entities.creeper.attacks`.
- `attacks = false` stops the damage to players only. The blast of a creeper
  still breaks blocks, as the game says, and still hurts other entities.
- A blast of TNT, of a bed and of `world.explode` has no kind. It follows the
  room's `damage` rule.
- The fields are for one room and one pack, as `spawn` is. If one pack sets
  `false`, the field is off.

To put mobs in a world, use [`world.spawn(name, pos)`](#ref-World-spawn) (see
[Mobs](#entities-mobs)), `/summon`, or a dungeon spawner the terrain placed.

> **Note:**
> a0.1.0 spawns nothing on its own. Only its dungeon spawner makes
> mobs.


## `game.terrain`

[`game.terrain`](#ref-Game-terrain) describes this world's overworld: `snow`,
and `steps` in the shape citadel.yml uses. It is read-only, and `nil` where the
engine has no list.

```luau
for i, step in ipairs(game.terrain.steps) do
  print(i, step.step, step.block, step.count)   -- 1 dungeons nil 8
end
print(game.terrain.snow)                        -- false
```

The step names and their keys are in
[Terrain generation](#world-terrain-generation--the-a010-terrain-steps).

## See also

- [Terrain generation](#world-terrain-generation) — the terrain steps the
  overworld runs, and where `game.terrain` comes from.
- [World state](#world-world-state) — the `survival` and `damage` rules that
  `drops`, `spawn`, `attacks` and `interact` resolve against.
- [Custom entities](#entities-custom-entities) — `game.entities.define` and `amend`
  for kinds of your own.
- [Mobs](#entities-mobs) — `world.spawn` and what mobs drop.

<!-- /world/world-state/ -->

<a id="world-world-state"></a>

## World state

> **In short:**
> the switches a pack flips on a room and the clocks it reads.
> `world.rules` turns the parts of the player simulation on and off —
> survival, fall, damage, hunger, anticheat, day_cycle and redstone — with
> strict boolean semantics. `world.time` holds or drives the sky, and
> `world.explode` and `world.spawn_point` finish the room-level world calls.


## `world.rules`

```luau
world.rules(opts: { survival: boolean?, fall: boolean?, damage: boolean?,
                    hunger: boolean?, anticheat: boolean?, day_cycle: boolean?,
                    redstone: boolean? }?) -> Rules
```

[`world.rules{ fall = true }`](#ref-World-rules) switches one on, `false` off.
A rule left out or `nil` keeps its value, and **a number or a string is an
error**: `world.rules{ fall = 0 }` and `world.rules{ fall = "off" }` stop the
script. [`world.rules()`](#ref-World-rules) with no argument reads them.

| Rule | What it runs |
| --- | --- |
| `survival` | the engine's survival — and it turns `fall`, `damage`, `hunger`, `anticheat` and `day_cycle` on |
| `fall` | fall damage |
| `damage` | hits and blasts hurt players |
| `hunger` | the food bar |
| `anticheat` | the movement and hit checks |
| `day_cycle` | the sun moves |
| `redstone` | signals move in the room |

A `mode: full` server has them all on; a pack can turn one off. On a pack
server they are all off until the pack says — except `anticheat` and `redstone`,
which are on everywhere until a pack turns them off.

### `survival`

`survival` gives the room to the engine's survival, as on a `mode: full`
server:

- A broken block drops its normal drops.
- A block the world breaks by itself drops them too: a torch whose wall is
  gone, a leaf that decays, a block an explosion or a piston breaks, sand that
  cannot land.
- Placing uses up the stack.
- The inventory and a crafting table craft.
- A death drops the inventory, and the respawn button works.
- The engine saves the player's inventory.
- It also turns on `fall`, `damage`, `hunger`, `anticheat` and `day_cycle`.

Without `survival`, a dig reaches no block, and a block the world breaks by
itself leaves no item. [`game.block(name).drops = true`](#ref-Block-drops)
switches one block of the game back on — see [Game data](#world-game-data). A
pack block still leaves the drops its definition lists; `drops = "table"` is
the game's own drop and leaves nothing.

> **Tip:**
> a survival pack puts `world.rules{ survival = true }` at the top, and
> runs the same on either kind of server.


<a id="world-world-state--redstone"></a>

### `redstone`

`redstone` is on in every room until a pack turns it off. With it off, no
signal moves: a lever lights no wire, a piston stays in, a pack block's `power`
gives nothing and `block.powered` reads `false`. What was lit when the rule
changed stays as it is until something beside it changes.

### `anticheat`

`anticheat` checks what each Java player's client claims:

- A player who flies, runs too fast, sends moves faster than the game ticks, or
  walks through full blocks goes back to the last legal position.
- A claim to stand on nothing does not prevent fall damage.
- A hit on something the player does not look at, or faster than 20 per second,
  does not land.
- After enough failed checks in a short time, the engine removes the player.
  The message names the check.
- The flight check skips creative and spectator players, a player who may fly
  (`player.can_fly`), a rider and a dead player.
- `player:push` and a movement effect (`speed`, `jump_boost`, `levitation`,
  `slow_falling`, `dolphins_grace`) exempt the player while they last.
  `player:teleport` is always allowed.

> **Gotcha:**
> a pack that moves players in any other way turns `anticheat` off:
> `world.rules{ anticheat = false }`.


### Anything else is the pack's job

Anything that is not a rule is the pack's job: `player:damage` for a hit,
`player.health` to heal, `players.on_death` and `players.on_respawn` for what
happens next, and `hit.player` in `players.on_click` for one player hitting
another:

```luau
world.rules{ fall = true }
players.on_click(function(player, hit)
    if hit.button == "left" and hit.player then
        hit.player:damage(2)
        hit.player:push(player:look() * 0.5 + vec3(0, 0.3, 0))
    end
end)
```

## The time of day

The time is in ticks, 0 at dawn and 24000 to a day. Each room has its own time,
and late joiners get the same sky.

```luau
world.time("night")          -- sets the hour: sunrise 23000, day 1000, noon 6000, sunset 12000, night 13000, midnight 18000
world.time(18000)            -- sets the hour, in ticks
world.time(function(s)       -- a cycle: asked each tick, s seconds after this call
    return 1000 + s * 40     -- a day of ten minutes, from morning
end)
world.time(function(s)       -- anything the pack likes: a day that stops at dusk
    return math.min(1000 + s * 20, 12000)
end)
local now = world.time()     -- 0 .. 23999
```

- A call replaces the previous one, a function too.
- The function returns ticks or a name. If it errors, the sky stays where it
  was.
- Whether the sun moves is a rule: `world.rules{ day_cycle = true }` runs the
  version's own day (20 minutes), and nothing else of survival.
- On a `mode: lite` world and in a room made by `rooms.create`, the rule is off
  and the sun stays straight overhead (noon).
- On a `mode: full` world, and after `world.rules{ survival = true }`, the rule
  is on.
- A number or a name sets the hour. With `day_cycle` on, the day runs on from
  there, as `/time set` does. With it off, the sky stays there.
- A function drives the sky itself. The engine's day stands aside until the
  next `world.time` call.

> **Note:**
> a stopped sky, the normal day or an `s * 20` day costs one packet a
> second. A faster or slower day costs one packet every tick it moves.


**Weather** is not a world call: a biome's `weather` field is the weather there
(see [Terrain generation](#world-terrain-generation--biomes)), and a dimension
turns it off with `type: { weather: false }`. The world's `level.json` keeps
the seed, spawn, time and weather of the first run.

## `world.explode`

```luau
world.explode(pos: Vec3, power: number?)
```

A blast at a point. The power is clamped by this game's own column and the
tick's explosion budget decides when it goes off, never whether. A blast of
`world.explode` has no kind — it follows the room's `damage` rule.

## `world.spawn_point`

[`world.spawn_point`](#ref-World-spawn_point) is where players arrive in this
room; writable, and the same value as the room's `spawn_point`.

- A write changes where a player arrives: on a join, on a respawn, and on a
  move to the room. The clients in the room get the new compass target.
- The write is **not stored**. After a restart the room has the point of
  `citadel.yml` or of the stored world again.
- The write does not move the chunks that stay loaded, the spawn protection, or
  the area where no mob spawns by itself. Those stay at the first point.

The full treatment, including `player.spawn_point` for a player's own respawn
point, is in [Rooms and dimensions](#concepts-rooms-and-dimensions--spawn-points-precisely).

## See also

- [Rooms and dimensions](#concepts-rooms-and-dimensions) — per-room tables, spawn
  points, dimensions.
- [Game data](#world-game-data) — the `drops`, `spawn`, `attacks` and `interact`
  fields that resolve against these rules.
- [Custom blocks](#world-custom-blocks) — `block.powered` and pack block power,
  which `redstone` switches off.
- [Terrain generation](#world-terrain-generation) — biome weather.
- [Health](#players-health) — what `damage` and `fall` mean for a player.

<!-- /world/spatial-queries/ -->

<a id="world-spatial-queries"></a>

## Zones, raycasts and paths

> **In short:**
> the world answers three kinds of spatial question. **Zones**
> watch a box and tell you who entered. **Raycasts** ask what a line hits —
> one at a time or a thousand in buffers. **`world.path`** asks how a mob
> walks from A to B. Around them: `world.sees` for line-of-sight,
> `world.light_at` for light, `players.near`/`players.within` for proximity.


## Zones

```luau
local goal = world.zone{
    from = vec3(10, 64, 10), to = vec3(14, 66, 14),
    on_enter = function(player) message(player.name .. " scored", colors.lime) end,
    on_leave = function(player) end,
}
goal:contains(player)     -- boolean
goal:players()            -- who is in it now
goal:destroy()
```

The rules:

- `from` and `to` are block positions, in either order; both corners are
  inside.
- A player is inside when their **feet** are.
- Disconnecting inside a zone runs `on_leave`.
- A zone ends with the script — make it again on reload.

## Raycasts

```luau
world.raycast(from, direction, 32)   -- the first block a ray meets within 32 blocks, or nil:
--   { block = vec3, face = "up" | "down" | "north" | "south" | "west" | "east" }
world.raycast(player.at + vec3(0, 1.62, 0), player:look())   -- what the player is looking at
```

- Returns the block position and the face the ray came in through; `nil` for
  no hit.
- The ray starts at `from` and runs along `direction` up to `max` blocks.

`world.sees(from, to)` answers the binary question — true when no block stops
the line between the two points:

- It looks as a mob looks: a block with a **collision box** stops the line —
  glass and leaves too. Water, lava, grass and flowers do not.

## Batched raycasts

`world.raycasts(rays, out, n)` casts `n` lines at once, through buffers:

- `rays` is a buffer with **six f64 for each line**: from x, y, z, then to
  x, y, z.
- `out` gets **one f64 for each line**: how far from `from` the first
  stopping block is, or `-1` when the line is clear.

> **Tip:**
> one call for all the bodies of an `on_think` is much cheaper than
> one `world.raycast` each. The same collision rules apply as `sees`.


## Pathfinding

`world.path(from, to, opts)` is the game's own search for a mob:

```luau
local points = world.path(from, to, { size = { 0.6, 1.95 } })
-- the points a body walks, a list of vec3, or nil
```

| Option | Meaning | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `size` | A number, or `{ width, height }` | 0.6 by 1.8 |
| `swim` | `true` to go through water | off |
| `fall` | The most blocks it may fall | 3 |
| `range` | How far it may go from the goal | the distance plus 16 |
| `budget` | The most blocks it looks at | 2000 |

- The search takes four ways from each block, a step up of one block, a fall
  of at most `fall` blocks. It gives the middle of each block to walk on,
  from `from` to the block at `to`.
- A search that stops early gives the part that came closest. `nil` when it
  found no step at all.
- A path costs the pack, not the tick: a short one costs microseconds; a long
  one around a big wall costs more. Ask for a new one when the old one is
  old, not each think.

## Light

```luau
local block, sky, open = world.light_at(pos)
-- block light 0..15, sky light 0..15, and true when no block above stops the sky
```

`world.light` is different — a client-side light *source* a pack places (see
[Displays](#ui-displays)); `world.light_at` reads the real light of a
position.

## Who is near

```luau
players.near(pos, 8)       -- every player within eight blocks of a point
players.within(from, to)   -- every player inside a box of blocks, corners included
```

Both return handles you can use directly. For a watched area with callbacks,
use a zone; for a one-off check, use these.

## See also

- [Teleport pads](#cookbook-cookbook-teleport-pads) — zones put to work.
- [Custom entities](#entities-custom-entities) — `on_think`, where batched
  raycasts pay off.
- [Block reference](#world-block-reference) — `world.light_at` in context.

<!-- /entities/custom-entities/ -->

<a id="entities-custom-entities"></a>

## Custom entities

> **In short:**
> Every entity has an `on_steer` and an `on_tick` hook, and
> three calls reach them: **amend** the game's own entity, **define** your
> own, and **spawn** it. This page is the full `game.entities.define`
> specification — looks, physics, size, the living body with its health,
> drops and sounds, hit volumes, flying and swimming, and the `on_think`
> brain — plus `game.entities.amend` for the game's own kinds, deadlines,
> and two packs on one kind. The handle they all hand you is
> [Entity handles](#entities-entity-handles).


## The three verbs

Call `define` and `amend` **while your pack loads** — a definition is a fact
about the world. `world.spawn` puts either kind at a point.

| Call | Returns | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`game.entities.amend`](#ref-Entities-amend) | — | Change the hooks of one of the game's own kinds |
| [`game.entities.define`](#ref-Entities-define) | `EntityDef` | Make a kind of your own |
| [`world.spawn`](#ref-World-spawn) | `EntityHandle?` | Put an entity of either at a point |

## Amending the game's own

An amend changes the **hooks** of a kind the game ships:

```luau
game.entities.amend("pig", {
    on_steer = function(e, base)
        base(e)            -- vanilla wander
        e.jumping = true   -- but always jumping
    end,
})
```

The amend also changes **pigs already in the world**, with no respawn.

- `base` is the behaviour you wrap: vanilla's, or the previous pack's.
- `base` makes a *decision*. What you assign after it wins. Two calls act as one.
- Wrapped behavior runs first by default. To replace it, pass `{ replace = true }` as the third argument and omit `base`.
- An amend changes **hooks** only. It refuses the keys `size`, `looks`, `physics`, `max_health`, `speed` and `persist`. For an entity that looks different, use `define`.
- You can amend only **the game's own** content. A name with a colon is refused.

`game.entities.pig:amend(hooks, options)` is the same call in another
spelling. The options — `priority`, `replace` — are
[`EntityAmendOptions`](#ref-EntityAmendOptions); see
[Two packs on one kind](#entities-custom-entities--two-packs-on-one-kind).

## Defining a kind of your own

`define` takes an [`EntitySpec`](#ref-EntitySpec) and hands back an
[`EntityDef`](#ref-EntityDef) you pass to `world.spawn`. A rocket with a
fuse:

```luau
local rocket = game.entities.define {
    name = "rocket", looks = "tnt", physics = "falling", size = 0.98,
    on_tick = function(e)
        e.velocity = e.velocity + vec3(0, 0.12, 0)
        e.data.fuse = (e.data.fuse or 60) - 1
        if e.data.fuse <= 0 then
            local at = e.at
            e:destroy()
            world.explode(at, 4)
        end
    end,
}

local it = world.spawn(rocket, vec3(8.5, 66, 8.5), { fuse = 40 })
```

### The EntitySpec fields

Every field of the spec, as the source documents it:

| field | what it is |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | your name for the kind. The engine adds the namespace: `"rocket"` becomes `"rave:rocket"`. You cannot use another pack's namespace. Lower case letters, digits and underscores. |
| `looks` | a shape the client **already draws**: `"pig"`, `"tnt"`, `"item"`, `"falling_block"`, `"none"`. Two forms take a payload: `{ entity = "falling_block", block = "sand" }` and `{ entity = "item", item = "diamond" }`. A name that this game's oldest client does not know is refused, never replaced. |
| `physics` | the movement order: `"living"`, `"falling"`, `"item"`, `"none"`. Not a table of numbers; the game version sets those. `"living"` is a body with health: see [a living body](#entities-custom-entities--a-living-body). |
| `size` | one number, or `{ width, height }`. Depth equals width, so a third number is an error. |
| `persist` | `"save"`: it comes back with the chunk, `e.data` included. Or `"despawn"`, the default. |
| `looks = models.x` | a model a pack made, with `seats`, `scale` and `fallback` next to it. See [Displays and 3D models](#ui-displays). |
| `physics = "vehicle"` | the engine drives it by seat 1's keys, with `speed`, `turn`, `accel`, `step`. See [Displays and 3D models](#ui-displays). |

> **Gotcha:**
> a world opened without your pack **quarantines** your entities:
> nothing ticks or shows them, and saves keep them unchanged. Install the
> pack again and they continue.


### The lifecycle hooks

`world.spawn` gives a pack's own kind the `data` it starts life holding
(`{ fuse = 40 }` above); a game mob kind takes none. Three notifications
follow — the engine never waits on them, and their return value is not read:

| hook | told when |
| --- | --- |
| `on_spawn(e)` | one of this kind is spawned |
| `on_load(e)` | one that already existed comes back: a saved chunk loaded it or a reload rebound it |
| `on_remove(e, why)` | it goes. `why` is `"removed"`, `"settled"`, `"killed"` or `"unloaded"`; `"killed"` after a death |

With `persist = "despawn"` (the default) the entity goes away when no player
is near, as a mob does; with `"save"` it stays, with its health and `data`.

<a id="entities-custom-entities--a-living-body"></a>

## A living body

With `physics = "living"` the entity is a real living thing. It falls, walks,
steps up half a block, swims, and takes fall damage, with the numbers of the
game version. It has health, players can hit it, and it dies. It has no mind
of its own: it moves only as your hooks say.

```luau
local sheep = game.entities.define {
    name = "fluffy", looks = "sheep", physics = "living", size = { 0.9, 1.3 },
    max_health = 8,                       -- 20 if you leave it out
    speed = 3,                            -- blocks a second at forward = 1
    drops = { { item = "white_wool", count = { 1, 3 } }, { item = "mutton" }, { item = "diamond", chance = 0.05 } },
    sounds = { hurt = "entity.sheep.hurt", death = "entity.sheep.death", ambient = "entity.sheep.ambient" },
    on_steer = function(e)
        e.forward = 1                     -- walk
        e.rotation = { yaw = -90 }        -- east
        e.jumping = e.data.stuck == true  -- jump when you ask it to
    end,
    on_damage = function(e, amount, by)
        if by then e.data.angry_at = by.name end
    end,
    on_remove = function(e, why)          -- why is "killed" after a death
    end,
}
world.spawn(sheep, vec3(8.5, 66, 8.5))
```

| field | what it is |
| --- | --- |
| `max_health` | the most health it has, and what it starts with. A whole number from 1 to 1024. 20 by default. `e.max_health` reads it. |
| `speed` | how fast it walks at `forward = 1`, in blocks a second. By default, the game's own mob walk (about 3). |
| `drops` | what it leaves when it dies. Each row is `{ item = "stick", count = 2 }`. `count = { 1, 3 }` gives a random count. `chance = 0.05` leaves the row after one death in twenty; without it, after every death. A row can be a pack item. `false` or nil: nothing. |
| `sounds` | `{ hurt = ..., death = ..., ambient = ... }`, each a vanilla sound or `"<pack>.<file>"`. Each one is optional. |
| `can_fly` | `true`: it may fly, and it takes no fall damage. Your pack sets `e.flying` to take off and to land. See [flying and swimming](#entities-custom-entities--flying-and-swimming). |

- These five keys need `physics = "living"`. On another physics they are an error.
- Steer with the intent fields: `e.forward`, `e.strafe` (-1 to 1), `e.jumping` and `e.rotation.yaw`. A body keeps its intent until you change it. For AI, write them from `on_think`: see [a brain](#entities-custom-entities--a-brain).
- Writing `e.velocity` still works. It is a push by hand.
- A whole block needs a jump: set `e.jumping`, as a mob does.
- A player's hit hurts it as a mob: the same damage, knockback, a red flash and a short time in which a second hit does not land. Arrows, falls, fire, lava and drowning hurt it too.
- `on_damage(e, amount, by)` is asked before a player's hit lands. `by` is that player. Answer `"ignore"` to stop the hit. Other damage lands without the question.
- At 0 health it dies as a mob: it falls over, leaves its `drops`, and is gone a second later. `on_remove` gets `"killed"`, and `world.on_entity_death` fires.
- With `looks = models.x`, the model flashes red too, for half a second, on clients from 1.21.4. It stays red while it dies. Older clients do not see the model flash.
- With `looks = models.x` clients from 1.19.4 can hit it: the engine gives it an invisible hitbox of its `size`. Older clients cannot hit a model. A long model needs hit volumes.

### Hit volumes

A body's `size` is one square box. A long animal is much longer than that, so
a player who swings at its head or tail hits nothing. Give the model hit
volumes with `part:hitbox(from, to)`, in model units like a box:

```luau
local rex = models.new("rex", function(m)
    local skin = m:material("skin", colors.green)
    local body = m:part("body")
    body:box(vec3(-4, 6, -8), vec3(4, 16, 8), skin)
    body:hitbox(vec3(-4, 6, -8), vec3(4, 16, 8))          -- the body
    local head = body:part("head")
    head:box(vec3(-3, 10, -20), vec3(3, 16, -8), skin)
    head:hitbox(vec3(-3, 10, -20), vec3(3, 16, -8))       -- the head, in front (-z)
    local tail = body:part("tail")
    tail:box(vec3(-2, 8, 8), vec3(2, 12, 24), skin)
    tail:hitbox(vec3(-2, 8, 8), vec3(2, 12, 16))          -- the tail, in two parts:
    tail:hitbox(vec3(-2, 8, 16), vec3(2, 12, 24))         -- a hitbox is square from above
end)
local t_rex = game.entities.define {
    name = "rex", looks = rex, scale = 4, physics = "living", size = { 3.2, 5.5 },
}
```

- A hit on any volume is a hit on the body: the same damage, `on_damage` and death.
- The engine measures reach and aim to the volume a player hit, not to the body's feet.
- A volume turns with the body's yaw and tips with its pitch. It does not move with an animation: it stays where the part is at rest.
- A volume is square from above: as wide as its longer side. Split a long thin part into several volumes.
- A model with no volumes is hit on one box of the body's `size`.
- Each volume is an entity on the client. A body that stands still sends nothing; a body that moves or turns sends one move a tick for each volume that moved.

<a id="entities-custom-entities--flying-and-swimming"></a>

### Flying and swimming

A body with `can_fly = true` walks like any body and flies when `e.flying` is
true. This bird walks, takes off, flies to a perch and lands:

```luau
local perch = vec3(20.5, 75, 8.5)
local bird = game.entities.define {
    name = "bird", looks = models.bird, physics = "living", size = { 0.5, 0.6 },
    speed = 6, can_fly = true,
    on_steer = function(e)
        local to = perch - e.at
        local far = math.sqrt(to.x * to.x + to.z * to.z)
        e.rotation = { yaw = math.deg(math.atan2(-to.x, to.z)), pitch = 0 }
        if e.data.landed then
            e.forward = 0                           -- sits on the perch
        elseif e.age < 60 then
            e.forward = 0.5                         -- walks first
        elseif far > 1 then
            e.flying = true                         -- takes off, flies to it
            e.forward = 1
            e.rotation = { pitch = math.deg(-math.atan2(to.y, far)) }
        else
            e.flying = false                        -- drops onto the perch
            e.forward = 0
            e.data.landed = true
        end
    end,
}
```

- `e.flying = true`: no gravity. `forward` and `strafe` move it along its look, `rotation.pitch` included: a negative pitch climbs, a positive one dives. At `forward = 1` it flies at its `speed` (by default the game's own air speed, about 4 blocks a second). With `forward = 0` it slows down and hovers.
- On the ground and still flying, it walks at its walk speed; a pitch up lifts it off.
- `e.flying = false`: it falls, lands, and walks again.
- A body with `can_fly` never takes fall damage, as the game's own fliers do, also when you move it with `e.velocity`.
- `e.flying = true` on a body without `can_fly` is an error. `e.flying` reads `false` there.
- **In water** every body swims along its look. A pitch up rises as fast as a jump in water does, a pitch down dives. At pitch 0 it swims and sinks as a mob does. Its speed in water is the game's swim speed, not `speed`. A flying body does not sink in water.
- `e.in_water` is `true` while it is in water: a crocodile can walk on land and swim when it is in.
- Clients see the pitch: a `looks = models.x` model tips with it (clients from 1.19.4); a vanilla look turns its head.

<a id="entities-custom-entities--a-brain"></a>

## A brain

AI is pack code, and it lives in `on_think`. The engine gives the numbers and
applies the answers. It does not walk to a point or attack for you. Use
`on_think` for AI, not `on_steer`: the engine waits for `on_steer` two
milliseconds each tick, and a slow pack loses that decision — it never waits
for `on_think`, and it never loses its answer.

```luau
--!native
local zombie = game.entities.define {
    name = "walker", looks = "zombie", physics = "living", size = { 0.6, 1.95 },
    think_every = 0.25,                 -- seconds; each body thinks 4 times a second
    on_think = function(b)              -- one call for all the due bodies of this kind
        for i = 0, b.n - 1 do
            local o = i * 8             -- body i of a column is at byte i * 8
            local dx = buffer.readf64(b.player_x, o) - buffer.readf64(b.x, o)
            local dz = buffer.readf64(b.player_z, o) - buffer.readf64(b.z, o)
            buffer.writef64(b.yaw, o, math.deg(math.atan2(-dx, dz)))
            buffer.writef64(b.forward, o, if buffer.readf64(b.player, o) ~= 0 then 1 else 0)
        end
    end,
}
```

- `b.n` is the number of bodies in this call. Each other field of `b` is a `buffer` with one number (an f64, 8 bytes) for each body. Body `i` is at byte `i * 8`, for `i` from 0 to `b.n - 1`. A yes or no is 1 or 0. An id of nothing is 0.
- The engine sends the bodies after a tick. The answer goes on the bodies at the start of the next tick that has it: one tick later, or more for a slow pack. An answer is never dropped. A slow pack is never switched off.
- To change a value, write a new one. A value that you do not change stays as the body has it. A body keeps its intent until you change it.
- `think_every` is seconds, above 0 and at most 60. Without it, each body thinks each tick. The engine spreads the bodies of a kind over the ticks.
- An event makes a body think on the next tick, also when it is not due.
- `b` and its buffers are the same table and buffers in each call. Their numbers change. Keep your own memory in a table by `id`.
- `on_think` cannot wait: `task.wait` in it is an error.
- `on_think` is for `define`. `amend` refuses it. A kind without it costs nothing.
- `--!native` at the top of the file makes this loop fast where the server allows native code. The buffers are the form native code reads fastest.

The [`Think`](#ref-Think) columns, one buffer each:

| column | what it is |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | the entity id, as `e.id` and `world.entities()` give it |
| `x`, `y`, `z` | where its feet are |
| `health`, `age` | its health, and the ticks it has lived |
| `on_ground`, `in_water` | 1 or 0 |
| `hurt` | the damage it took since its last think; 0 for none |
| `hurt_by` | the id of the player whose hit it was; 0 for none |
| `landed` | 1: it came down on the ground after it was in the air |
| `blocked` | 1: it walked into a wall |
| `water` | 1: it went into water; -1: it came out; 0: neither |
| `touched` | the id of a player it began to touch; 0 for none |
| `player` | the id of the nearest player in survival or adventure; 0 for none |
| `player_x`, `player_y`, `player_z`, `player_dist` | where that player's feet are, and how far |
| `yaw`, `pitch` | where it looks. Write to turn it. |
| `forward`, `strafe` | its intent, -1 to 1. Write to walk. |
| `jumping`, `flying` | its intent, 1 or 0. `flying` is for a body with `can_fly`. |
| `vx`, `vy`, `vz` | its velocity. Write to push it by hand. |

- Each event is in one think only. The next think has it at 0 again.
- `citadel.budget().asks.kinds.think` counts the bodies: `asks` sent, `answered` applied, `late` applied more than one tick after they were sent. `missed` stays 0.
- Use `on_steer` only for an answer in the same tick, such as a vehicle that turns on a key. It can miss.
- Outside a hook, `e.forward`, `e.strafe`, `e.jumping` and `e.flying` on a world handle change the body at once.

### A small steering library

The engine has no `move_to`. Copy this into your pack and change it as you
need. It turns smoothly, follows the points of `world.path`, jumps when a
wall blocks it, and aims a flier up or down.

```luau
--!native
-- steer.luau
local steer = {}

-- `from` turned toward `to` by at most `step` degrees.
function steer.turn(from: number, to: number, step: number): number
    local d = (to - from + 180) % 360 - 180
    return from + math.clamp(d, -step, step)
end

-- The yaw that looks from (x, z) to (tx, tz).
function steer.yaw(x: number, z: number, tx: number, tz: number): number
    return math.deg(math.atan2(-(tx - x), tz - z))
end

-- The pitch that flies up `dy` over `far` blocks: negative climbs.
function steer.pitch(dy: number, far: number): number
    return -math.deg(math.atan2(dy, far))
end

-- Body i of `b` walks the route { points = world.path(...), at = 1 }.
-- false when it is at the end.
function steer.follow(b, i: number, route, turn: number?): boolean
    local o = i * 8
    local x, y, z = buffer.readf64(b.x, o), buffer.readf64(b.y, o), buffer.readf64(b.z, o)
    local p = route.points[route.at]
    while p and (p.x - x) ^ 2 + (p.z - z) ^ 2 < 0.3 and math.abs(p.y - y) < 1 do
        route.at += 1
        p = route.points[route.at]
    end
    if not p then
        buffer.writef64(b.forward, o, 0)
        return false
    end
    local yaw = steer.turn(buffer.readf64(b.yaw, o), steer.yaw(x, z, p.x, p.z), turn or 45)
    buffer.writef64(b.yaw, o, yaw)
    buffer.writef64(b.forward, o, 1)
    local up = p.y > y + 0.5 or buffer.readf64(b.blocked, o) == 1
    buffer.writef64(b.jumping, o, if up then 1 else 0)
    return true
end

-- A flier of `b` aims at (tx, ty, tz): it flies there and looks up or down.
function steer.fly(b, i: number, tx: number, ty: number, tz: number)
    local o = i * 8
    local x, y, z = buffer.readf64(b.x, o), buffer.readf64(b.y, o), buffer.readf64(b.z, o)
    local far = math.sqrt((tx - x) ^ 2 + (tz - z) ^ 2)
    buffer.writef64(b.flying, o, 1)
    buffer.writef64(b.yaw, o, steer.turn(buffer.readf64(b.yaw, o), steer.yaw(x, z, tx, tz), 30))
    buffer.writef64(b.pitch, o, steer.pitch(ty - y, far))
    buffer.writef64(b.forward, o, if far > 1 then 1 else 0)
end

return steer
```

A chaser with it. It asks for a new path each second, or when it has none:

```luau
local steer = require("steer")
local routes = {}                       -- by body id
local chaser = game.entities.define {
    name = "chaser", looks = "zombie", physics = "living", size = { 0.6, 1.95 },
    think_every = 0.1,
    on_think = function(b)
        for i = 0, b.n - 1 do
            local o = i * 8
            local id = buffer.readf64(b.id, o)
            local r, age = routes[id], buffer.readf64(b.age, o)
            if buffer.readf64(b.player, o) == 0 then
                buffer.writef64(b.forward, o, 0)
            elseif not r or age > r.renew then
                local from = vec3(buffer.readf64(b.x, o), buffer.readf64(b.y, o), buffer.readf64(b.z, o))
                local to = vec3(buffer.readf64(b.player_x, o), buffer.readf64(b.player_y, o), buffer.readf64(b.player_z, o))
                routes[id] = { points = world.path(from, to, { size = { 0.6, 1.95 } }) or {}, at = 1, renew = age + 20 }
            end
            if routes[id] then steer.follow(b, i, routes[id]) end
        end
    end,
    on_remove = function(e) routes[e.id] = nil end,
}
```

## What a missed deadline means

Your hooks run outside the tick. Each tick, the engine sends your pack **one
batch** with all your due entities. It waits two milliseconds, then applies
the answers: `on_steer` before physics, `on_tick` after. The contract:

- **a hook reads the entity as it was at the start of that tick**; and
- **for custom kinds or `{ replace = true }`, a missed deadline keeps the last intent.** The entity keeps steering the same way. The miss is counted at `citadel.budget().asks.kinds["entity"].missed`.

| hook | a missed deadline means |
| --- | --- |
| `on_steer`, `on_tick` | Default amendments continue wrapped behavior. Custom kinds and explicit replacements keep their last intent; physics runs anyway. |
| `on_think` | nothing is missed: the engine does not wait. A slow answer lands on a later tick. See [a brain](#entities-custom-entities--a-brain). |
| `on_damage` | **`"take"`**: the damage lands. A busy pack must not make its own entities invulnerable. |
| `on_spawn`, `on_load`, `on_remove` | the engine never waits on these. They are notifications, and their return value is not read. |

- `on_remove` does **not** fire when your pack is removed.
- A reload is not a missed deadline. If the new script no longer amends a kind, the kind gets its wrapped behaviour back. Your own kinds, fuses included, keep moving through a reload.

<a id="entities-custom-entities--two-packs-on-one-kind"></a>

## Two packs on one kind

Amendments run in an explicit order, not the load order:

- Use `game.entities.amend(name, hooks, { priority = 10, replace = false })`. Amendments run from lower to higher integer priority, regardless of pack name or load order. Priority defaults to `0`.
- Two packs amending the same kind at the same priority produce a load error naming both packs; choose distinct priorities explicitly.
- By default, wrapped behavior runs first, even if the hook omits `base` or misses its deadline. Calling `base(e)` remains supported and never runs it twice.
- Set `replace = true` explicitly to allow the hook to suppress the wrapped steering/tick behavior; with this option, calling `base(e)` opts back into it. The same options work with `game.entities.pig:amend(hooks, options)`.
- Custom kinds made with `define` retain their existing `base` behavior.

## Pack kinds and mob kinds

What `define` hands back, and where it sits among the game's own kinds:

- `define` hands back an `EntityDef` — the kind's `name` and `mob = false` — usable anywhere the name is: pass it to `world.spawn` just like the string. A pack kind (`rave:rocket`) reads the same from `game.entities`.
- A kind is a **mob** when the game gives it health and a mind of its own: a cow, a zombie. An arrow, an item and a boat are not mobs. A player is not an entity here: players are in `players`, never in `world.entities`. The facts of a game kind are in [Game data](#world-game-data).
- Profiles — a mob's native behaviour values — are read-only; a write raises an error, and a special behaviour without a shared profile returns `nil`. Profiles run no callbacks. To change gameplay, use `game.entities.amend(name, hooks)` and `game.entities.define(spec)`.
- The values a pack writes — `spawn`, `attacks`, `interact` — are for one room and one pack. `game` is the main room's table. A room from `rooms.create` has its own: `room.game.entities.cow.spawn = true`. The full rules are in [Game data](#world-game-data).

## See also

- [Entity handles](#entities-entity-handles) — the handle `world.spawn` returns and every hook receives: `at`, `velocity`, `:push`, queries, `e.data`.
- [Mobs and spawning](#entities-mobs) — `world.spawn` on the game's own kinds, natural spawn rules and drops.
- [Game data](#world-game-data) — reading a kind's facts; the `spawn`, `attacks` and `interact` tri-states in full.
- [Displays and 3D models](#ui-displays) — `models.new`, vehicles driven by seat 1, seats and fallbacks.
- [Runtime](#concepts-runtime) — pack load, reload semantics and the tick budget.

<!-- /entities/entity-handles/ -->

<a id="entities-entity-handles"></a>

## Entity handles

> **In short:**
> A handle is a live view of **a body the world moves** — a
> pack's own entity, a mob, a stack on the ground. `world.spawn` returns one,
> `world.entities()` lists them, and each hook gets one. A mob has the same
> handle as every entity the world moves: `cow.velocity`, `cow:push(v)` and
> `cow:nearby(8)` all work. Every read is a fresh look at the world, so check
> `alive` before you trust what you read.


## What a handle is

The [`EntityHandle`](#ref-EntityHandle) is the one type behind every body the
world moves — a pack's own entity, a mob, a stack on the ground. Wherever you
get one from, it behaves the same:

- `world.spawn` returns a handle; `world.entities()` lists handles; each hook (`on_steer`, `on_tick`, `on_spawn`, ...) gets one.
- Every read is a fresh look at the world. A handle to something that has died reads `nil` on its fields — so **check `alive`** before you use what you read.
- Inside a hook, the same handle reads the entity as it was at the top of the tick, and its writes land at that hook's own slot.
- `tostring(cow)` is `entity(cow, 7)`: the kind's name and the id.

<a id="entities-entity-handles--position-and-rotation"></a>

## Position and rotation

`at` is where its feet are; `rotation` is which way it faces. Both are live —
set them and the entity is there:

| Read / call | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `entity.at` | where it is, live; writing it is a teleport. `nil` once it is gone. |
| `entity.rotation` | a table of degree angles. Bodies have no roll: yaw and pitch. Partial writes preserve omitted angles; `nil` after removal. |
| `entity:move(at, rotation?)` | sets position and optional rotation together. |

- 0 yaw faces south (+z), 90 faces west; positive pitch tips down. For a living body, `e.rotation.yaw` is one of the intent fields: it keeps the heading until you change it.
- `move` changes position and rotation in one operation, and validates both before applying either. Entities keep simulating after a move: changing their position does not clear velocity.
- Writing the current position with `at` or `move` is the normal way to place an entity; the engine smooths visual movement.

<a id="entities-entity-handles--velocity-push-and-intent"></a>

## Velocity, push and intent

There are two ways to move a body by hand — a shove now, or an intent it keeps
— and the intent fields are the ones steering uses:

| Field / call | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `entity.velocity` | how it is moving, live; writing it is steering by hand — a push. `nil` once it is gone. |
| `entity:push(v)` | a shove, in blocks a tick, added to what it is already doing. |
| `entity.forward`, `entity.strafe` | intent, -1 to 1. `strafe` is 1 left, -1 right. |
| `entity.jumping` | intent: whether it wants to jump. |
| `entity.flying` | intent, a living body with `can_fly` only: `true` flies, `false` falls and walks. |

- A body keeps its intent until you change it. Outside a hook, writing `e.forward`, `e.strafe`, `e.jumping` and `e.flying` on a world handle changes the body at once.
- `e.flying = true` on a body without `can_fly` is an error; `e.flying` reads `false` there.
- A vehicle's seat 1 writes `forward`, `strafe` and `jumping` from the keys every tick. See [Displays and 3D models](#ui-displays).
- `entity.in_water` is `true` while it is in water.

## Finding entities

`world.entities()` with no argument returns all entities. For a local query,
give a position and a radius. You can also filter by kind:

```luau
local cows = world.entities {
    near = vec3(8, 65, 8),
    radius = 16,
    kind = "cow",
}
for _, cow in cows do
    cow:push(vec3(0, 0.1, 0))
end

local allCows = world.entities { kind = "cow" }
```

| Option of `world.entities(query)` | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| — (no argument) | all entities |
| `near`, `radius` | a sphere, boundary included. They go together. |
| `kind` | the handle's canonical name, with the pack namespace for a custom kind |
| `mob` | `true`: the mobs only; `false`: the rest |

- Results are handles in ascending id order. Queued spawns are included; removed entities are not.
- Invalid options, a negative radius and non-finite numbers raise an error. An unknown kind returns an empty list.
- `entity:nearby(radius)` measures horizontal distance and excludes the entity itself.

## The fields

What a handle reads, beyond position and movement above. Most go `nil` once
the entity is gone:

| Field | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | its entity id, the one `players.on_click` reports in `hit.entity_id` |
| `name` | the kind's name: `"cow"`, `"rave:rocket"`. `nil` once it is gone. |
| `alive` | whether it is still in the world. A hook only runs for one that is. |
| `age` | ticks lived. |
| `at`, `rotation` | where it is and where it looks; see [position and rotation](#entities-entity-handles--position-and-rotation) |
| `velocity` | how it is moving; see [velocity, push and intent](#entities-entity-handles--velocity-push-and-intent) |
| `forward`, `strafe`, `jumping`, `flying` | the intent fields |
| `on_ground` | whether it stands on something. `nil` once it is gone. |
| `in_water` | `true` while it is in water |
| `health` | its health now. `nil` once it is gone. |
| `max_health` | the most health its kind gives it. Read-only; `nil` for an entity that is not a mob and once it is gone. |
| `hostile` | whether its kind is hostile. `nil` once it is gone. |
| `physics` | which order of operations moves it: `"vehicle"`, `"living"`, `"falling"`, `"item"` or `"none"` |
| `origin` | the block it used to be, for anything that arrived through a transition; `nil` for anything that was never a block |
| `data` | a pack-defined entity's attached record; see below |
| `driver` | the player supplying driving input from seat 1; `nil` for an NPC or empty seat |
| `paint` | material name to colour; write-only |

A model entity (a kind with `looks = models.x`) also has `scale` — `nil`
without a model — and the animation calls `entity:play(animation, { speed = n })`
and `entity:stop(animation)`: `play` starts a model animation from the start,
and on the one already playing only changes its speed; `stop` leaves the parts
where they are.

## e.data

`e.data` is a data view for a **pack-defined entity**, including one with
`physics = "living"`:

- Nested writes persist through both callback and world handles. It saves with the chunk only when the kind has `persist = "save"`.
- Reading or assigning `.data` on a **built-in entity**, including an amended one, raises an error: its engine-owned state is not a pack data record.
- Keep temporary state for built-in entities in a pack table keyed by entity id; ids do not provide a persistent identity across server restarts.
- `on_steer`/`on_tick` data views expire after the callback batch; copy out what you need to keep a snapshot.

## Amending reaches live entities

An amend is not a respawn: `game.entities.amend("pig", { ... })` changes
**pigs already in the world** the moment it runs, and every pig after, with no
respawn. The hooks change; the entities stay. What an amend cannot change —
`size`, `looks`, `physics`, `max_health`, `speed`, `persist` — and the
wrapping of `base` are in [Custom entities](#entities-custom-entities).

## Life, death and removal

The end of an entity is a read like any other — `alive` goes `false`, the
other fields `nil` — with two calls and two events around it:

- `entity:destroy()` removes it.
- `entity:settle()` stops it being an entity: it is a block again where it stands. No argument: the entity remembers what it was (its `origin`).
- A living body at 0 health dies as a mob: it falls over, leaves its `drops`, and is gone a second later. `on_remove` gets `"killed"`, and `world.on_entity_death` fires with its id and name.
- `world.on_entity_spawn` tells after a mob appeared, with its handle and name; a natural spawn fires it on every game version that has one, and a pack's own `world.spawn("cow", pos)` fires it too. Mob kinds only.
- `on_remove` is told `"removed"`, `"settled"`, `"killed"` or `"unloaded"`. It does **not** fire when your pack is removed.

## See also

- [Custom entities](#entities-custom-entities) — `define` and `amend`, the hooks, the `on_think` brain.
- [Mobs and spawning](#entities-mobs) — `world.spawn` on the game's own kinds, natural spawning, drops.
- [Displays and 3D models](#ui-displays) — vehicles, seats, and the shared `id`/`alive`/`at`/`rotation`/`:move` contract.
- [Game data](#world-game-data) — a kind's facts from `game.entities.<kind>`.
- [The event model](#concepts-events) — `world.on_entity_spawn`, `world.on_entity_death` and the other `on_*` subscriptions.

---

<!-- /entities/mobs/ -->

<a id="entities-mobs"></a>

## Mobs and spawning

> **In short:**
> A mob acts on its own on both kinds of server, lite included.
> `world.spawn(name, pos)` puts a mob — or a kind your pack defined — at a
> point and hands back the same handle every entity gets. Whether a kind
> spawns by itself is the per-kind `spawn` value; what it leaves behind is
> `drop` (or your own `drops` list). An NPC is not a mob: it does not survive
> a reload.


## What a mob is

A kind is a **mob** when the game gives it health and a mind of its own: a
cow, a zombie. An arrow, an item and a boat are not mobs. A player is not an
entity here: players are in `players`, never in `world.entities`.

- `game.entities.cow` and `game.entities.Cow` are the same kind; a kind that this game does not have is `nil`.
- `world.entities { mob = true }` lists the mobs only; `{ mob = false }` the rest. The facts of each kind — `max_health`, `width`, `height`, `speed`, `drop`, `hostile` — are on [Game data](#world-game-data).

## Spawning with world.spawn

`world.spawn(def, pos, data?)` puts an entity at a point and returns its
handle:

```luau
local cow = world.spawn("cow", vec3(8.5, 66, 8.5))    -- the game's own entity
local it = world.spawn(rocket, vec3(8.5, 66, 8.5), { fuse = 40 })  -- a pack kind, with its data
```

- A mob kind of the game by name (`world.spawn("cow", pos)`) is the game's own entity, and takes no `data`.
- A pack's own kind takes the data it starts life holding.
- `nil` for a kind nothing defined and this game does not have.
- `world.on_entity_spawn` tells after a mob appeared, with its handle and name; a natural spawn fires it on every game version that has one, and a pack's own `world.spawn("cow", pos)` fires it too. Mob kinds only.

> **Gotcha:**
> a0.1.0 spawns nothing on its own. On an Alpha world every
> entity in `world.entities { mob = true }` comes from a dungeon spawner,
> `/summon` or this call.


## A mob acts on its own

A mob needs no pack code to live its life, whatever the server runs:

- A mob acts on its own on both kinds of server, lite included.
- Each read gets the entity's current state. Check `alive`.
- A mob a pack spawns stays when the script reloads. An NPC does not — see [NPCs](#entities-npcs).

## The same handle

A mob has the **same handle** as every entity the world moves: `cow.velocity`,
`cow:push(v)` and `cow:nearby(8)` work too. `tostring(cow)` is
`entity(cow, 7)`: the kind's name and the id. The full handle API — position
and rotation, velocity and push, intent fields, `e.data`, queries — is
[Entity handles](#entities-entity-handles).

## Natural spawning: the spawn value

`spawn` is the field of a mob kind that a pack writes. It says whether the
kind is in this world by itself:

| Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `true` | The kind is in this world as the game defines it. It spawns by the game's own rule, and it is the game's entity in full. |
| `false` | The kind never spawns by itself. |
| `nil` | The pack sets nothing. The world's default applies. |

- The world's default is off on a `mode: lite` world and in a room made by `rooms.create`: no mob spawns by itself. The default is on on a `mode: full` world and after `world.rules{ survival = true }`.
- `false` stops natural spawning only. A spawner block, `world.spawn`, `/summon` and breeding still make the entity. Mobs already in the world stay.
- The value is for one room and one pack. `game` is the main room's table; a room from `rooms.create` has its own: `room.game.entities.cow.spawn = true`. If one pack sets `false`, the kind does not spawn.
- On a game with no natural spawning, every write is an error, `nil` included. a0.1.0 to a0.1.3 are such games.
- `true` makes the kind the game's entity in full, on a lite world too: its hits hurt players and a player's right click has the game's effect, unless a pack sets `attacks` or `interact`.

The full rules — per-world defaults, the `attacks`/`interact` fields and how
`nil` resolves against the room's rules — are in
[Game data](#world-game-data).

## Drops

What a death leaves behind is a fact of the kind, read from `game.entities`,
or a list your pack writes on its own kinds:

- `game.entities.cow.drop` reads the item a mob kind's death leaves behind — `"leather"` for a cow; `nil` for none.
- A pack-defined living body lists its own `drops`: rows of `{ item = "stick", count = 2 }`, `count = { 1, 3 }` for a random count, `chance = 0.05` for a row that comes from one death in twenty. See [Custom entities](#entities-custom-entities).
- A game **block's** `drops` — whether a block leaves its item when the world breaks it by itself — is a separate `true`/`false`/`nil` field of a game block, also in [Game data](#world-game-data).
- `world.on_entity_death` tells after a mob died; it is gone, so its id and name is all there is. Mob kinds only.

## See also

- [Custom entities](#entities-custom-entities) — `game.entities.define` in full: the living body, its `drops`, and amending mob behaviour.
- [Entity handles](#entities-entity-handles) — the handle a mob hands you: `velocity`, `:push`, `:nearby`, `alive`.
- [Game data](#world-game-data) — the `spawn`, `attacks` and `interact` tri-states in full; a kind's facts.
- [NPCs](#entities-npcs) — the player-shaped entity that does not survive a reload.
- [World state](#world-world-state) — `world.rules`: the `survival` and `damage` rules behind the spawn defaults.

---

<!-- /entities/npcs/ -->

<a id="entities-npcs"></a>

## NPCs

> **In short:**
> `world.npc{...}` places a player-shaped entity every client
> from 1.8 sees: skin, name tag, poses, walking, items in hand, armour,
> riding. The engine removes a script's NPCs when the script ends or reloads —
> a mob survives that, an NPC does not. `world.puppet{...}` places a mob's
> body with no mind of its own that the script moves.


## Making an NPC

`world.npc{...}` takes the options in one table: name, place, rotation and
skin. The skin has three forms, and the name has a length limit:

```luau
local n = world.npc{ name = "Dealer", at = vec3(0.5, 65, 4.5), rotation = { yaw = 180, pitch = 0 },
                     skin = "Notch" }   -- a player's name; the engine looks the skin up
--   skin = { value = "...", signature = "..." } is the raw profile property, for a skin no account wears
--   leave skin out, or write false, for the default skin; any other value is an error
```

| Option | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | at most 16 characters. |
| `at`, `rotation` | where it stands and which way it faces; set them later and the NPC moves. |
| `skin` | a player's name (the engine looks the skin up), `{ value = ..., signature = ... }` (the raw profile property), or left out / `false` for the default skin. Any other value is an error. |

- **Leave `name` out and the NPC has no name tag** from 1.8 on. A 1.7 client still shows a tag with an engine-made name.
- A `skin` given as a player's name costs two calls to Mojang. The NPC shows its own skin until the answer arrives. If no account has that name, the log says so.
- An NPC stays in the tab list for two seconds after it appears, then leaves it.

## The Npc API

Every call and field on the handle [`world.npc`](#ref-World-npc) returns, as
the docs list them:

```luau
n.id                   -- entity id, what players.on_click reports in hit.entity_id
n.name                 -- "" for one made with no name
n.at, n.rotation   -- live; set them and the NPC moves
n:look_at(pos)         -- turns head and body toward a point
n:swing()              -- the arm animation
n:hold("paper")        -- item in the main hand; n:hold(nil) or n:hold(false) empties it; errors on an unknown item
n:say("Place your bets.", "light_purple")   -- a chat line "<Dealer> ..." to the room (just the words with no name); text
n:walk{ path = { vec3(4.5, 65, 0.5), vec3(4.5, 65, 9.5) }, speed = 1.4, loop = true }
--   walks the points by itself, facing where it goes; speed in blocks a second
n.walking              -- true until the last point (never, with loop); n:walk(nil) stops it
n.pose = "sleeping"    -- "standing", "crouching", "sleeping" (flat on its back), "swimming" (flat on its front); live
n:wear{ head = "iron_helmet", chest = { item = "leather_chestplate", dye = colors.red } }   -- see "armour"
n:ride(car, { seat = 2 }) -> boolean   -- sits as player:ride does; false when that seat is taken
n:dismount()           -- gets off where it sits
n.riding               -- boolean, live
n:destroy()
```

The calls in table form:

| Call | Returns | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `npc:look_at(pos)` | — | Turn head and body toward a point |
| `npc:swing()` | — | The arm animation |
| `npc:hold(item)` | — | Item in the main hand; `nil`/`false` empties it |
| `npc:say(text, color?)` | — | A chat line `"<name> ..."` to the room |
| `npc:walk{ path, speed, loop }` | — | Walk the points by itself |
| `npc:wear(pieces)` | — | Armour, head first |
| `npc:ride(thing, { seat = n })` | `boolean` | Sit as `player:ride` does; `false` when the seat is taken |
| `npc:dismount()` | — | Get off where it sits |
| `npc:move(at, rotation?)` | — | Set position and rotation together |
| `npc:destroy()` | — | Remove the NPC |

The fields: `n.id` (the entity id), `n.name` (`""` for one made with no
name), `n.at` and `n.rotation` (live; set them and the NPC moves), and —
live — `n.walking`, `n.pose` and `n.riding`.

`n:hold` and `n:wear` take items like any other item call — the armour pieces
are in [Inventory](#players-inventory). `n:say` sends a chat line; its text
follows [text formatting](#ui-ui-basics), and its second argument is a
colour ink.

## Walking

The engine moves a walking NPC along the path the script gives once. It faces
its direction and moves its legs.

- It walks straight between points, at the points' height. Put points up a stair and at each corner.
- It walks through anything. The pack keeps the path clear.
- `n.walking` is true until the last point (never, with `loop`); `n:walk(nil)` stops it.

## Poses

A **pose** stays during a walk or a ride. A client that cannot show a pose
sees the NPC standing. `"standing"` is the default; the other
[`NpcPose`](#ref-NpcPose) values arrive with the client versions:

| pose | shown from |
| --- | --- |
| `"crouching"` | 1.8 |
| `"sleeping"` | 1.8: lying on its back, feet at `at`, head toward the yaw's side (to a quarter turn before 1.14) |
| `"swimming"` | 1.13 |

> **Gotcha:**
> for a client before 1.14, the engine puts a bed under a
> sleeping NPC, at height 0 in its column. Do not lay a sleeping NPC where
> the pack builds at height 0 in that column.


## Riding

`n:ride(thing, { seat = n })` takes what `player:ride` takes: a vehicle's
seat, a model display's seat, a display, a hitbox, or another NPC.

- Every client, also a later one, sees the NPC seated and moving with the vehicle.
- A client that cannot see the seat (a display needs 1.19.4) sees the NPC standing at the seat, moving with it.
- `ride` stops a walk. `n.at` reads the seat's position.
- An NPC never drives a vehicle — see [Displays and 3D models](#ui-displays).
- After `n:dismount()`, set `n.at` to move the NPC somewhere else.

`npc:ride` mirrors `player:ride`; the player-side rules — seats, `locked`,
what a mount takes — are in [Movement](#players-movement).

## Puppets

A puppet is a mob's body with no mind of its own that the script moves, from
[`world.puppet`](#ref-World-puppet). Its name tag is always shown:

```luau
local p = world.puppet{ kind = "horse", at = vec3(0.5, 65, -100.5), rotation = { yaw = 90 }, name = { "Lightning", color = "gold" } }   -- name is text
p.id, p.name           -- the name tag is always shown; errors when this game has no such mob kind
p.at, p.rotation   -- live
p:destroy()
```

- `kind` is required; it errors when this game has no such mob kind.
- `name` is text: `p.name` reads the name tag's text, which is always shown.
- Displays, model displays, NPCs, puppets and entity handles share `id`, `alive`, `at`, `rotation` and `:move(at, rotation?)` — the shared contract is on [Entity handles](#entities-entity-handles).

## NPCs and reload

The engine removes a script's NPCs and puppets when the script ends or
reloads. That is the line between an NPC and a mob:

- A mob a pack spawns stays when the script reloads; an NPC does not — see [Mobs and spawning](#entities-mobs).
- A puppet is a mob's body with no mind of its own; an NPC is player-shaped. Both are placed, moved and removed by the script.

## See also

- [Mobs and spawning](#entities-mobs) — `world.spawn` and what survives a reload.
- [Entity handles](#entities-entity-handles) — the shared `id`/`alive`/`at`/`rotation`/`:move` contract.
- [Displays and 3D models](#ui-displays) — vehicles, seats and what an NPC can ride.
- [Inventory](#players-inventory) — items and armour, what `n:hold` and `n:wear` take.
- [Movement](#players-movement) — `player:ride`, the calls `npc:ride` mirrors.

<!-- /players/player-lifecycle/ -->

<a id="players-player-lifecycle"></a>

## Player lifecycle

> **In short:**
> a player is one Luau value for as long as they are connected —
> every event hands you that same value, and your own state lives on it as
> `player.data`. Four events mark the path: join, leave, death and respawn.
> One twist: the global `players` table and a room's own `room.players` fire
> `on_join` at different moments. Nothing of `data` survives a rejoin, so
> persist what matters in `storage`. A player can also leave for another
> server entirely, with `player:connect`.


## Joining and leaving

Which table you subscribe on decides when the event fires.

- The global [`players.on_join`](#ref-Players-on_join) fires **on connect**, in
  the main room. A room's own `room.players.on_join` fires **on each move
  into it** — after every `player:move_to(room)`.
- `players.on_leave` matches: the same player value `on_join` had; it can no
  longer be sent to.

```luau
room.players.on_join(function(p) end)  -- fires after move_to as well
print(player.room == room)             -- rooms compare by identity; nil while moving
```

> **Note:**
> On a script reload, `players.on_join` runs again for every online
> player. Make it safe to run twice.


## The four events

Every lifecycle subscription returns a connection; `connection:cancel()`
unsubscribes (see [The event model](#concepts-events)).

| Event | Callback | Fires |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`players.on_join`](#ref-Players-on_join) | `(player)` | A client connects (global table); each move into a room (room's table). |
| [`players.on_leave`](#ref-Players-on_leave) | `(player)` | The same player value `on_join` had; it can no longer be sent to. |
| [`players.on_death`](#ref-Players-on_death) | `(player?, cause, message, by?)` | A player dies; `player` is nil once they have left. |
| [`players.on_respawn`](#ref-Players-on_respawn) | `(player?)` | A player respawns; `player` is nil once they have left. |

Delivery is guaranteed where it matters:

- Joins, leaves, deaths and respawns are retained in order and never evicted
  by ordinary traffic or skipped because the tick budget was spent. They carry
  the original player session, so a delayed leave still has its `player.data`
  after a reconnect.
- This is in-process delivery, not a durable journal across a server crash.
  Keep lifecycle callbacks short so their retained backlog drains.

> **Note:**
> The tick budget does not cover `players.on_join` — input events and
> task threads keep the 100 ms runaway limit instead. See
> [Runtime](#concepts-runtime).


## Death: cause, message, by

`cause` in `players.on_death` says what killed them:

| Cause | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `fall`, `drown`, `suffocate`, `void`, `lava`, `fire`, `cactus`, `starve` | The environment. |
| `attack` | A mob's or a player's hit. |
| `shot` | An arrow. |
| `blast`, `magic` | An explosion, magic. |
| `other` | A pack's own `player:damage`. |

`message` is the broadcast English death line. `by` is the player who hit or
shot them, or `nil`. What happens at zero health — and what does not — is on
[Health and damage](#players-health).

## A player is one value while connected

Every event passes the same `player`:

- `a == b` compares players, and a player can be a table key.
- `player.data` holds your own state. You need no table keyed by name.

The identifying fields:

| Field | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `player.name` | The player's name. |
| `player.uuid` | The account's own id: the one name for a player a rename does not change. |
| `player.at` | Where they stand now. |
| `player.room` | The Room the player is in; nil while they move between rooms. |
| `player.data` | Your own table, kept on the player for as long as they are connected. |

## player.data

`data` is the per-session state holder: your own table on the player, gone
when the player is.

- In `players.on_leave`, `player.name` and `player.data` still read. `data` is
  kept for 10 seconds after they leave; after that a value you still hold
  reads an empty table.
- `data` may name the player (`p.data.state = { player = p }`, a function that
  uses `p`); it is let go with them all the same.
- A player who rejoins is a new value with empty `data`.

```luau
players.on_join(function(p) p.data.coins = 0 end)
players.on_leave(function(p) storage.set("coins." .. p.uuid, p.data.coins) end)
```

> **Gotcha:**
> Nothing in `data` survives a reconnect. A rejoining player is a
> new value with empty `data` — and a new session resets the session settings
> too (hidden players, `visible`; see
> [Visibility and teams](#players-visibility)). Write what matters to
> [storage](#systems-storage) in `on_leave` and read it back in `on_join`.


## Leaving for another server

[`player:connect(server)`](#ref-Player-connect) asks Minefort's proxy to move
the player: a BungeeCord `Connect` for a Java player, a `Transfer` to that
name for a Bedrock player. It returns nothing and does not yield.

| `server` is | The player goes to |
| --- | --- |
| an instance's `id` | that instance (see [Network](#systems-network)) |
| the network's name | its default member; `network.info().network` is that name |
| `hub` | Minefort's hub |

The fine print:

- The name is 1 to 128 characters of letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`. Any
  other name is an error, and nothing is sent.
- Minefort decides. It does not move a player to a server out of the network,
  and it does not tell the pack.
- The call does not tell the pack the result. A player who is still here some
  seconds later was not moved.
- It moves a Bedrock player, and a Java player on 1.7 or later. A Java player
  on an older version stays.
- On a local run there is no proxy. A Java player stays. A Bedrock client
  reads the name as an address, and leaves the server.

## See also

- [Health and damage](#players-health) — death causes, respawn and the damage calls.
- [Movement and cameras](#players-movement) — `move_to` and rooms in context.
- [Visibility and teams](#players-visibility) — what a new session resets.
- [Storage](#systems-storage) — persisting per-player state across sessions.
- [The event model](#concepts-events) — connections, cancellation and budgets.
